item.title: Cellesignalering
item.description:
There are four basic forms of communication between our cells Endocrine (hormonal) communication Paracrine (And autocrine) Neuronal Contact-Dependent Endocrine signalling ... Paracrine signalling Short distance (local) communication using multiple local mediator molceules - an important one being growth factors This also includes autocrone signalling, which means that the cell it self is affected by its own signalling molceulesNeuronal
Neurotransmitters and RecptorsContact-Dependent Communication between cells, where membrane bound signal-molecules are recognizes by membrane bound receptors (b-cells , etc.)Many signalling molecules are used in the endrocrine communication - that is all the hormonesParacrine signalling molecules are typically growth factors (GF) but also other moleculesNeuronal signalling are mediated by neurotransmittersContact-Dependent signalling are by delta molecules
The contact point of a signalling molecules is often dependent on its polarity. Hydrophil molecules usually bind on cell-surface recepters (Small) Hydrophobic molecules usually bind to intra-cellular recepters Some of the hormones being able to diffuse across the membrane or being translocated across it:
These are all transcription regulators. When the corresponding receptors are in the cytosol they are inactivated By binding to the given ligand, they activate forming the receptor-cortisol complex These translocate to the nucleus Here they ...
There are three groups of receptors Ion channel-coupled receptors G-protein coupled receptprs Enzyme-coupled receptors The same ligand can activate multiple different receptors. This means that different types of cells react differently to the same signalling molecules Looking at acetylcholine it can Decrease heratrate in pacemaker cells Activate secretion in salivary gland cells Initiate contraction in skeletal muscle cells There are two principles behind receptor activated signalling (from the membrane) That...
For many of the receptors, the ligands are called first messengers, which initiates a pathway that transduce/amplify second messengerSignalling sometimes functions as a molecular switch. This means that the signal can turn on/off a given protein. This have two mechanisms Protein phosphorylation by the signaling activated protein kinase activating the protein GTP-binding proteins which can be activated by the signalling activating the GTP binding
When the delta signal protein makes contact with the delta receptor (notch), the notch tail is cleaved intracellularly, which can act as a transcription regulator.

item.title: RNA Processing
item.description: All RNA is processed in some way, but it is mainly the mRNA, that goes through the full proces. RNA polymerase I synthesizes pre-rRNA with no cap, no polyadenylation and some self-splicing RNA polymerase I synthesizes pre-rRNA with 7-methylguanosin cap, cleaving and addition of polyadenyl tail and ribozyme catalyzed intron removal (spliceosomes) RNA polymerase III synthesizes pre-tRNA and 5S rRNA with no cap, no polyadenylation and some enzyme-catalyzed intron removal The processing takes place in the nucleus for eukaryotes, while in the cytosol for prokaryotes (no nucleus). The processing from nascent mRNA to mature mRNA occurs co-transcriptionally, that is it begins while the the mRNA is being synthesized.

item.title: Transcription to RNA
item.description:
The first step in the gene expression is the transcription of DNA to RNA or ribonucleic acid.Like DNA, RNA is a linear polymer of of nucleotide subunits. It differs in two ways The nucleotides are called ribonucelotides because they contain ribose as their sugar instead of deoxyribose RNA contains the base uracil instead of thymine, which is chemically similar, and it forms the same double hydrogen bond to adenine Structurally they differ quite a lot, as RNA doesn't form double strands, but stays in single strands, which means that it like can fold in a myriad of ways, just like polypeptide chains. This allows RNA to carry out functions it self, and not just function as an information carrier.
There are multiple types of RNA with different functionsMessenger RNA (mRNA) is the RNA that the majority of genes code for. mRNA usually carries information from one gene, to be translated to a single protein. (In bacteria one mRNA can code for multiple proteins). 1-2% of the transcribed RNA Noncoding RNA is all the RNA that aren't translated to proteins. This is subdivided into multiple types it self: Ribosomal RNA or rRNA forms the structural core of the ribosomes and are thus very important is this allows the translation of mRNA. 80% of the transcribed RNA Transfer RNA or tRNA selects specific amino acids and holds them in the place of the ribosome where they are to be incorporated into the protein 10% of the transcribed RNA MicroRNA or miRNA is a part of the regulation of gene expression Small nuclear RNA og snRNA is a part of the processing of pre-mRNA. Many other types of noncoding RNA The transcription is quite similar to DNA replication. Roughly described the processes is: The DNA strands are disassociated in a given place Here the RNA polymerase begins sequentially adding ribonucleotides to a strand complementary the the nucleotides on one of the DNA strands, by mending the phosphodiester bonds of the RNA backbone. The energy for the reaction is given by the ribonucleotides (ATP, CTP, UTP and GTP) The RNA chain is elongated in the 5' 3' direction, just like in replication After being appended to the chain, the nucleotide and complementary ribonucleotide disassociate, and the DNA strands reassociates, while the RNA strand remains one-stranded. The product is called the RNA transcript.
RNA polymerase is different and somewhat simpler than DNA polymerase. It doesn't need a primer to begin the transcription process There is no proofreading mechanism to correct errors, because the RNA is not permanent information storage, so it doesn't have as big consequences. This means that an error occurs for every nucleotide Because the RNA disassociated so rapidly, and the DNA helix reforms, there can be multiple transcriptions of the same gene overlapping. For a medium-sized gene of 1500 bp, there can be dozens of RNA polymerase transcribing at the same time, allowing more than 100 RNA transcripts to be produced in an hour Often however, it is much less In eukaryotic cells there is not one but three types of RNA polymerase, each responsible for different types of RNA RNA Polymerase I is responsible for most ribosomal RNA RNA Polymerase II is responsible for the mRNA, miRNA and some other noncoding RNAs RNA Polymerase III is responsible for tRNA, some rRNA and other RNAs The focus throughout is on RNA Polymerase II The transcription always begin at a promoter. The promoter is a gene region with specific sequences, that lies upstream of the starting point (The promotor is not transcribed). Because of the asymmetry of the promoter, it will only be recognized in one direction, which will start transcription in the 5' 3' direction (reading the complementary 3' 5' strand). The terminator is a similar gene region with specific sequences, that terminates the transcription at the stop site just after the terminator (and thus the terminator is transcribed). In prokaryotic cells the promoter is recognized by the sigma unit of the polymerase, which is released upon the beginning of transcription, and then rebound after the RNA polymerase is released from the DNA, activating it for a new transcription. Here the promoter is given by consensus sequences in the -35 and -10 spot (relative the the start of transcription).
In eukaryotic cells the sequences of the promoter is recognized by different general transcription factors. We have the following regions recognized by consensus sequences: TFIIB recognizes a sequence at -35 TBP recognizes a sequence at -30 This concists of mostly T and A nucleotides - know as the TATA box TFIID recognizes a sequence at 0 (transcription start site) TFIID recognizes a sequence at +30 TFIIH?!
Because of the asymmetry of the promoter it is directional. This means that it can be present in both directions of the DNA, and gene transcription can take place on the 3' 5' strand in both directions.
In order to initiate the eukaryotic transcription, we require a set of general transcription factors to form the initiation complex. Firstly the TBP subunit of the TFIID binds to the TATA box This cause a distortion in the DNA double helix, forming a kink in the helix TFIIB binds to create a bridge to RNA Polymerase II which binds together with TFIIE and -F Lastly TFIIH joins with two subareas serving different functions The helicase part dissociates the strands at the transrciption start site. The kinase part which phosphorylates the tail of the RNA pol II Together they form the transcription initiation complex (The chronological order differs) In order for the transcription to commence, it must be released from the complex. This happens with the phosphyrylation of the pol II tail, which releases most of the general transcription factors, which is then available for reuse.
After dissociating the general transcription factors, multiple elongation factors joins the RNA polymerase II. These factors help the pol II move along the DNA, and they allow pol II to acces the DNA in the nucleosomes, by unwrapping it from the histones.
Interestingly the mRNA slicing and further processing to mature mRNA occurs co-transcriptionally, that is it begins while the nascent mRNA is being synthesized.
Once the pol II reaches the polyadenylation signal it is released from the mRNA. One released, the tail must be hydrolyzed before it can be used again.

item.title: DNA Mutations and Repair
item.description:
Tags: #CellBiology #Genetics DNA is constantly damaged with 10,000 to 100,000 damages to the DNA per cell per day. Given cells in a human this is quite a lot. We have a DNA repair system fixing most of these damages, but some make it through - mutations. Whether the mutations happens to somatic cells or gametese (Kønsceller) makes a lot of difference, as mutations in a somatic cell can lead to individual disease, but mutations in gametese (or precursor cells) can lead to disease (maybe precancer mutations) for every child. DNA Repair Mechanisms These have kept most of the genes safe for millions of yearsThe important mechanisms: Proofreading Mismatch repair Excision repair Homolog recombination Non-homolog endjoining If DNA is damaged to prospects could be Celle death (e.g. apoptosis) Cancer by the mutations Genetic diseases Evolutionary (fordele?) Mutations in somatic cells are only dangerous to our selves.The possible sources of damages can be divided into two categoriesEndogen Errors in DNA replication Spontanious in the cell because of metabolism Exogen UV and radioactivity Chemical Some of the resulting damages include Lack of a base Modification of a base Wrong base pair Base-dimers (Covalent binding of bases) Breakage of one or both strands DNA polymerase makes 1 mistake for every 100,000 nucleotides. This is quite a lot, but the polymerase proofreading and mismatch repair we get to 1 in nucleotidesThe first correction mechanism is done by the DNA polymerase when synthesizing the strand. This is called proofreading. This is done by another domain on the polymerase, than the one performing polymerization. Just before placing a new nucleotide, the polymerase "checks" whether the bases are a match, and if not, it clips off the mispaired nucleotide and tries again. This is only possible because of the direction of the synthesis. If it were to be synthesizes in the 5' direction, then the removal of the wrong nucleotide would result in the strand being blocked by a phosphate. If the error gets past proofreading we can get a mismatch (Wrong nucleotide pairing). If such a mismatch is left for further replication, we get different DNA helices with correct parings, but mutated sequences:
For fixing these wrong nucleotide pairings we have the mismatch repair system The problem is to identify which strand is the correct strand, that is the original strand. This is possible because there is a difference between the strands just after synthesis. There is gaps between the DNA fragments, that have not yet been mended by DNA ligase. Mismatch repair proteins identifies a hole and scan the newly synthesized strand til it finds an error (A mismatch) It then removes the entire segment from the error to the hole, which can then be recreated correctly by the DNA polymerase.
Damages not only happen during replication, but also spontaneously. One spontaneous error is depurination (Depurinering) where the -glycoside binding is hydrolyzed, and the base is released from the nucleotideAnother is deamination (Deaminering) where an amine group is removed from the base - swapped with a ketone - changing it into another base - Adenine is deaminated to Guanine, or Cytosine is deaminated to Uracil
A particularly tough deamination to fix is when 5-methyl-cytosine is deaminated to thymine. Which is almost never fixed.This is damages, that aren't spontaneous, but happens as a result of UV, radiation, and chemicals such as in cigarettes, nitrate and nitrite preservative, and barbecuing. Particularly UV results in thymine dimers. This is a result of two neighboring thymines forming a covalent bond, which for example will stall the replication process at the affected side. This can in fact happen for all prydimidines (Cytosine, Thymine and Uracil)
When damage happen to only one of the strands, we use excision repair. This includes multiple processes given the particular damage, but the general process is in three steps The error is cleaved (excised) from the DNA (Nuclease activity) The repair DNA polymerase fills in the missing part using the other strand as template A DNA ligase fills in the nick/gap The two specific processes used (Excluding Mismatch repair): Base excision repair happens when there occurs a mismatch between the bases in the base pair - for example after depurination Specific glycalases removes the base AP endonuclease removes the backbone DNA polymerase synthesizes a new correct fragment DNA ligase closes the nick Nucleotide excision repair is when there occurs thymine dimers Endonuclease cleaves the DNA backbone around the affected area Helicase removes the affect DNA DNA polymerase synthesizes a new correct fragment DNA ligase closes the nick If both strands are damaged / cleaved, we have no intact template strand to repair the DNA. There are two mechanisms for fixing this.Nonhomologous end joining can happen always after an accidental double strand break. It is simply to quickly join the exposed ends together before they drift apart. Nuclease processes the DNA end, often removing nucleotides in order to align the ends. Specialized DNA ligase joins the end together This results in a repaired DNA string, with some loss of bp and thus mutations Homologous recombination can only be used when there is an undamaged DNA clone nearby (Shortly after replication) The undamaged DNA can be used as a template We don't need to understand the details! Recombination-specific nucleases processes 5' ends of the two exposed DNA ends. Rad52 guides to 3' end to the aligning part of the non-damged DNA strand, where it can be extended by DNA polymerase The same thing occurs for the other fragment DNA Ligase merges the nick Results in a fully repaired DNA with no loss of bp
Many mutations are usually needed to have any real effect, but sometimes single mutations can have en effect on its own A single mutation in a valine in the -globulin gene results in mutated hemoglobin and strokes Looking at the single nucleotide level we have Insertions - A new nucleotide inserted Deletion - A nucleotide is removed Base-change When wee look at how these mutations affect the codons we have in importance ranking Nonsense - Encoding a stop codon Missense - Resulting in a different amino acid Synonymous - Resulting in the same amino acid by chance When looking at the reading frame we have Frameshift mutations where a number of nucleotides thats not a product of 3 is added/removed - Thus changing every codon Inframe mutations, where the number is a multiple of 3, thus affecting the amino acids in the affected codons, but not shifting the reading frame. In protein coding genome, some point mutations doesn't change the protein at all E.g. AAG (Coding for lysine) -> AAA (Also coding for lysine) Some of the worst mutations are genes coding for the proteins involved in the DNA repair it self: Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) Werner syndrome Breast- and ovary cancer (BRCA1/2) Prostata cancer (BRCA2) When the DNA repair proteins fail, the mutations can accumulate far quicker - especially two types of mutations leads to cancerous cells Oncogenes are genes that if mutates leads to uninhibited cell division Tumor supressor genes are genes that supresses uninhibited cell division, but if mutated can't inhibit the tumor.

item.title: Translation to Proteins
item.description:
Translation is the process of translating mRNA to proteinsRibosomes are an important part of the translation. A polysome is a series of ribosomes that simultaneously translates the same mRNA molecule leading to many copies of the translations in a short interval of time. This is why we see the christmas tree-like structures in a miller spread The ribosome it self consist of a large subunit and a small subunit The large subunit consists of 3 rNA molecules and 39 ribosomal proteins (MW=2,800,000) The small subunit consists of 1 rNA molecules and 33 ribosomal proteins (MW=1,400,000)
There are differences between eukaryotic and prokaryotic ribosomes The size of the subunits differ in a way, that creates structural change, meaning that we can design antibiotics, that targets only the units of the prokaryotic ribosome. The location also differes, where the prokaryotic ribosomes are mostly in the cytosol, the eukaryotic are both in the cytosol and the ER The ribosome has three tRNA binding sites called A - Aminoacyl site P - Peptidyl site E - Excit site
The ribsome is in itself a ribozyme, meaning that it is an RNA molecule with catalytic activity (opposed to enzymes, which must be translated from mRNA first) The RNA in the large subunit catalyzes peptide bonding at the P site - (specifically the ribozyme peptidyl transferase) The catalytic activity is dependent on the RNA folding correctly (secondary and tertiary structure) The tRNA molecules match the amino acids to codons in the mRNA. The tRNA is trascribed by the RNA polymerase III, unlike the mRNA. There are 64 possible codons 61 amino acid coding codons (Including the start codon "AUG" - Methionine) 3 stop codons The tRNA includes four double stranded segments by complementary base pairing The secondary structure forms a cloverleaf like shape, with three loops The tRNA folds into an L-shape (tertiary structure) The nucleotides on the tRNA matching the given codon on the mRNA is called the anticodon on the anticodon loop.T
The tRNA can not it self recognize and bond to the correct amino acids - This is the role of aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase, which catalyzes the peptide bond formation (between the carboxyl group of the amino acid and the tRNA 3' end) of the amino acid corresponding to the tRNA codon, using ATP hydrolyzis as energy. There is a version of aminoacyl-tRNA synthase for each amino acid - that means 20 versions
The translation of a complete polypeptide chain in an mRNA molecules has three steps Initiation Elongation Termination The translation always starts at "AUG" codon, followed by the coding sequence
In prokaryotes the AUG can occur multiple times on the mRNA making the prokaryotes polycistronic. This means, that prokaryotes don't rely of the AUG for starting, but has special ribosome-binding sites, upstream of each start codon.
Since the starting codon "AUG" also codes for the amino acid methionine, all polypeptide chains begins with this, but it is usually cleaved off. A special initiator tRNA (Met-tRNA) is needed to start the translation at the "AUG" codon. This initiator Met-tRNA is different from the normal elongation Met-tRNA, which cannot initialize the translation The initiator tRNA forms complex with the small ribosomal subunit and some translation initiation factors Before the initialization can commence, special proteins at the 5' cap and at the poly(A) tail is requiredThe complex binds to the mRNA at the 5' cap and scan for the first start codon. The first AUG thus defines the reading frame. When found, the initiator tRNA binds to the AUG, the translation initiation factors dissociate, and the large subunit binds with the initiation tRNA in the P site. This leaves the A site empty, for the second charged tRNA (with an amino acid bound)
Eukaryotes make monocistronic mRNAs, where only one protein / molecule is decoded, while prokaryotes make polycistronic mRNAs where multiple proteins can be decoded per mRNAAfter the start codon has been recognized, the initiation factors dissociate, and the large ribosomal subunit binds to the complex. Elongation herefrom commence in four steps A charged tRNA base-pairs with the codon in the A site In the in the P site, the C-terminus of the polypeptide chain uncouples from the tRNA and instead forms a peptide bond with the amino acid in the A site The large subunit shifts such that the P site becomes the E site, and the A site becomes the P site. Thus the A site is once again empty The small subjunit also shifts, ejecting the tRNA at the E site This sequence of action then repeats over and over.
The mRNA sequence is decoded into the codons along the translation process. Errors resulting in a missing or added nucleotide, can shift the entire reading frame, meaning that every resulting codon is different. Since the codons come in nucleotide triplets, there is three different reading frames or mRNA
When a stop codon enters the A site, it is bound by release factors instead of tRNA. The release factors adds an to the polypeptide chain, freeing the C-terminus of the chain. The ribosome then releases the mRNA and the different parts dissociate.
The final translated polypeptide is not yet the finished protein, as it must fold correctly, it can covalently bind to cofactors, it can by post-translationally modified, etc.At the end of life for proteins, the proteasomes break back the proteins into amino acids Short-lasting proteins Misfolded / damaged proteins It is signaled by polyubiquitin chains bound to the target protein. These Ubiquitinated proteins are unfolded and fed trough the central cylinder of the proteasomes, where the polypeptide chain is degraded into amino acids, and the ubiquitin is recycled.

item.title: Transcriptional and Post-Transcriptional Regulation
item.description:
Out genes consist og 1% Protein coding 20% Introns 30% Intergenic/Non-repetitive 50% Repetitive elements Why do we regulate genes? Gene expression is costly, and constant protein production is unecesary. We must adapt to the environment by switching specific genes on/off We wish to express specific genes for specific cell types We need developmental timing when going from embryo to adult We have a wide spectrum of gene regulation mechanisms, all of which varying in the resource cost as well as reaction speed (Inversly propertional ish) Transcriptional control RNA processing control mRNA location control mRNA degradation control Translation control Protein degradation control Protein activity control Transcription regulators Prokaryotic transcription regulation Eukaryotic transcription regulation Proteins can act upon and regulate the DNA transcription directly. There are many of these transcription regulators, many of which are transcription factors (but not all). During transcription the general transcription factors (Or Sigma factor for prokaryotes) bind to the (core) promoters, binding RNA polymerase and initializes transcription. In the upstream region of the promoters, there are regulatory promotor regions, where "ligangs?" can bind to activate or repress the general transcription factors.
The transcription factors interact with the major groove of the DNA, as the chemical information is more accessible. Here some chemical groups in the nucleotide bases are exposed. This allows for Hydrogen bonds Hydrophobic interactions Electrostatic interactions The different base pairs this provide different binding possibilites:
The transcription factors usually interact with the DNA in the form of -helices forming some of the structures Homeodomain Zinc fingers Leucine-zipper
Per -helix we can only bond to 2 or 3 base pairs, thus multiple -helices are usually needed to interact with the DNA.The transcription factors can bind in different places on the regulatory promoter region, having different effects on the transcription- all dependent on the genes and promotor regions them selves. Bacteria have a small genomes of merely 4 million bp. With only 4000 proteins, and 60% active at any time, they need to be very adapative to the environment in terms of gene expression. The genes in the bacteria are often arranged in OPERONs, in which multiple genes are expressed by the same promotor (and promotor region) - The result can be simultaneous synthesis of enzymes that act in the same pathway, called coordinated expression. This coordinated expression of the OPERON are controlled by a DNA segment called the operator. The operator can be activating / repressing dependent on the transcription factor bound to the operator. Example: The E.coli tryptophan operon - a binary switch When tryptophane is high, the tryptophane binds to the repressor, which is activated and binds to the operator, restricting the transcription When it is low, the repressor is inactivated, and releases the operator, allowing the RNA polymerase to transcribe the gene.
The eukaryotic gene regulation is more complex than the prokaryotic regulation. Many general transcription factors are needed for recruiting RNA polymerase, not just sigma factor Promoter regions can extend far upstream from the core promoter, also indirectly interacting with the RNA polymerase ... Additional regulatory regions can be further away the the promoter regions These are called the enhancers and the silencers. These are brought together with the promotor by mediator protein complexes The loops that restrict activity of expressers and silencers are formed by COHOSIN proteins. In general the eukaryotic regulation of transcription os a coordinated process, with many parts working together Promoters - The regions on the DNA that allows to Transcription factors - Enhancers (And silencers) - Mediator - The RNA Pol II - TADs -
The organization of the chromatin plays a role in the transcription ...While every cell in the body contains the same genome, we find that of the 20.000 protein-coding genes, only 50-60% are expressed 8-9k are shared between all cells 2-3k
By definition epigenetics refers to heritable, reversable changes in the gene functions that don't change the DNA sequence. The epigenome thus sits "on top" of the genome - a collection of the compounds and modifications to the chromatin that regulates gene expression without changing the underlying DNA sequence. The epicgenetic mechanisms are multiple Histone modifications DNA methylation Chromatin remodeling 3D genome organization Non-coding RNAs The histone modifications ...The DNA methylation is when the DNA methyltransferase (DNMT) ads a methyl group to the cytosine. TET enzymes does the opposite, removing the methyl group It only happens on the CpG sequences in the DNA. The DNA methylation happens all over, but it is especially important on promoters, where methylation blocks the transcription factors, effectively turning the gene off.
Or alternatively ...
When does the actual differentation between cells occur? Mostly during development, where cells go from totipotent - meaning, that it can differentiate to any specialized cell - to multipotent, and lastly unipotent cells. This means a decrease in developmental potential This also mean an increase in epigenomic complexity There is multiple steps of Post-Transcriptional Modifications, but our focus is on RNA PRocessing control mRNA degradation control Translation control After the transciription we have the pre-mRNA, which needs processing Splicing Capping Polyadenylation The mature mRNA also includes untranslated regions (UTRs) before the start codon, and after the stop codon. These play an important role in translocation, etc.
This gives os room for regulatory intervention. The UTRs include the 5' UTR before the start codon, and the 3' UTR after the stop codon.When translation begins, the small ribosome subunit binds to the mRNA cap, and searches for the start codon. RNA-binding proteins in the 5' UTR can block this search, and thus inhibit the translation Similar stem loops (hairpins) on the 5' UTR can slow down or inhibit the translation figur...In the 3' UTR we can regulate the stability of the mRNA. The poly A tail gives stability to the mRNA, by protecting the end. Over time the tail degradates, so the longer the poly A tail, the longer the time of stability The RNA location sequences, the zip code, is also in the 3' UTR Au rich elements?????? MicroRNA mediated repression Some types of RNA are used for translation (tRNA and rRNA). Some however regulates other types of RNA: Micro RNA (miRNA) Small interfering RNAs (siRNA) Long Non-coding RNAs (IncRNA) miRNA The most important regulatory RNA is the miRNA. We have about 2000 miRNA genes, and about 60% of human protein-coding genes are regulated by miRNAs. One miRNA can regulate hundreds of targets One mRNA contains mulitple miRNA binding sites Usually the binding takes place in the 3' UTR, but sometimes at CDS and rarely at 5' UTR. They primarily act as fine-tuners of gene expression, dampening protein output rather than completely silencing genes.The precursor miRNA (pri-miRNA) is transcribed like other genes by teh RNA polymerase II. It is then processed into short intermediates (pre-miRNA). This is loaded into the RISC complex. Scanning for complementary target Good mach -> mRNA is degradaded by nucleases within RISC Not as good a muach -> Translation reduced, mRNA sequestered and eventually degredaded by nucleases in the cytosol An example is the miR-15a/miR-16-1 in B-cells, which inhibits the BCL2 gene (anti apoptopic proteins), resulting in more apoptosis If the microRNA is removed (leuchemia), the BCL2 gene is not inhibited, and the apoptosis is blocked siRNA These are used in plants and "lower" animals as a defence mechanism, and are also used in reasearch to create gene knock-down effects (functional analysis). It can also be used in drugs During virus infection, cells are infected by foreign RNA. This is cleaved by DICER into double- stranded siRNAs. These form complexes with RISC proteins, which can degrade mRNA just as with miRNA.

item.title: DNA and Kromosomes
item.description:
Tags: #CellBiology #GeneticsThe nitrogen containing bases that are the fundamental part of the genome sequence, is divided into pyramidines and purines.
Dexoyribonucleic Acid (DNA) consists of two chains of nucleotides (not to be confused with nucleosides). In DNA the nucleotides consists of a deoxyribose bound to the given base by a -glycoside bond with one to three phosphates bound to the 5-carbon In RNA the it is ribose instead of deoxyribose - Thus the DNA nucleotide with adenine is called ATP, while the RNA nucleotide is called dATP
The nucleotides composing the strands are connected via phosphodiester bonds. The strands are thus polarized with the 5' end being the one with the exposed phophate, while the 3' end being the one with a 3-hydroxyl group on the deoxyribose
The nucleotides always exists in the same Watson-Crick Basepairs across the helix Thymine Adenine (Two hydrogen bonds) (In RNA Thymine is swapped with Uracil) Cytosine Guanine (Three hydrogen bonds)
The helix is formed by the hydrogen bonds between the base pairs. The strands are antiparallel meaning that the 3' end of one strand is next to the 5' end of the other. The distance between the strands is asymmetrical with the turning, meaning that one "turn" - (The major groove) is wider than the other (The minor groove) Each turn is 10.4 bp, and there is 0.34 nm between nucleotides, giving nm pr turn
The helix of the DNA can be denaturated (Locally split in two) and renatured again. This is an essential feature of the DNA.
Normally this is enzymatically catalyzed, but heat can also "melt" the strand connections. This not an absolut or linear process, but convergent - thus we define the melting temperature as the point of 50% of the strand (hydrogen bonds) being disassociated. is dependent on the number of hydrogen bonds which is determined by the ratio of A=T (Two bonds) to G=C (Three bonds) and the length of the DNA.
The genome is all the DNA in a given celle (and organism). The human haploid (Single chromosomes) genome consists of bp
The diploid human genome is divided in 46 chromosome pairs (Including the two x or x+y) Only a small proportion of the chromosomes (and genomes) are transcribed, and even less is translated to proteins. About 1.5% codes for proteins in the humane genome Not all genes code for protein, a gene is (loosely) defined as a segment of DNA that is transcribed.

There is 2 meters of DNA stuffed into in a nucleus of 10 . This is possible due to the structure and organization of the chromosomes.The basal fiber of the chromosomes is chromatin. This is this beads-on-a-string like fiber, with DNA sequentially wrapped around histones.The nucleasomes constists of DNA wrapped around large histones, as well as linker DNA linking the wrapped histones. There are 200 base pairs per nucleosome (including the linker of bp) This gives bp wrapped about the histone The nuuclease, MNase, can cleave the linker DNA releasing nucleosome core particles The MNase is activated by

The nucleosomes can be supplemented by histone H1 (Linker Histone) Unlike H2A/B, H3 and H4 it isn't part of the bead, but sits on top of it It locks the linker DNA in place, though to be condensating the chromatin
The chromatine is formed by the nucleosomes, which in turn forms the chromatine fiber of packed nucleosomes. This fiber is folded in loops to the mitotic chromosome This is 10,000 times shorter than the DNA length
All of the genome is present in every cell of the body (sort of). Then how the different cells express different types of functionEpigenetics! - The nucleosome position and chromatine structure is different between cell types. This can be controlled by transciption factors Because some parts of the chromatine is compact - heterocromatine , it cant be transcribed in contrast to euchromatine which is active This is how different cell types, can control which genes is transcribed - a lot if these being translated to proteins The figure shows how the chromatin structure allows two cells to express similar genes (Red) and different genes (Green and Purple)
The chromatine can be remodeled by remodeling complex, which can make condensed chromatin - decondenced Using ATP they modify the structure of nucleosomes and the overall structure of the chromatin
The N-terminal tails of the histones can be modified in a way, that modifies the conformation of the histones. There are very many possibilities for modifications If there is a lot of acetylisation, the histones are often decondensed The positively charged lysines are attracted to negatively charged DNA, leading to condensed chromatin When these are acetylated it leads to neutral charge, and thus less condensation Phosphorylation can both works for condensation and decondensation of chromatin Used commonly in DNA damage reparation Methylation can also both work for condensation and decondensation Lysine and arginine can be methylated A single lysine can have mono- di and tri-methylation Depending on the modiffications they can code for histone codes
An example of the complexity is trimethyl on the H3 tail, which results in heterochromatin formation and gene silencing - but if next to acetylation, it will lead to gene expression
Protein code readers binds to the different histone codes / modifications, which lead to Gene transcription DNA synthesis DNA repair The denser structure appears darker in the microscope, meaning that condenced chromatin that is not transcribed appear darker than the decondenced chromatin. In the following images we see a highly active transcription to the right, with plenty of decondenced chromatin (and a nucleolis in dark), while the left image shows an inactive transcription with a lot of condenced chromatin.
This is a process where the activity of a DNA segment can be changed, without changing the sequence. The methylation usually occurs on cytosine, but also adenine at times. The methylation of cytosin usually leads to gene silencing A part of the aging process Involved in hippocampal long term memory Cancer
The chromosomes has three regions of interest during the cell division Telomeres is the end part of every chromosome - Formed of heterochromatin, this is slowly degraded with age (and enough cell division) Replication origins is the place where the replication of the DNA begins during interphase Centromers is the site of assembly of the kinetochores during mitosis (Chromosome segregation) - Formed of heterochromatin

In a embryo cell, we see the epigenetic factors will inactivate one of the X chromsones (in biological females) Th entirety of the one chromosome is "inactive", which is passed on through cell division Thus only the genes of one of the X chromosomes are expressed This is controlled by acetylsation of the histones
We not only inherit genome, but also the chromatin structure and thus histone modifications

item.title: DNA Replication
item.description:
Tags: #CellBiology #Genetics The cells of the body is constantly multiplying and being replaced with a total of cell divisions in an average human life. Before each cell division, the DNA must be copied.The synthesis must only happen in the S phase of the cell cycle, but the processes leading to the replication can happen in earlier phases.More in the cell cyclus lecture
The DNA polymerase does 5' 3' synthesis of the DNA strands, that is it reads from 3' end to the 5' end (Defined by the "free" carbon in the dexoyribose"), and thus is synthesized the other way round: 5' 3'.
The synthesis are said to be semiconservative, as each new DNA helix is a result of one original strand and one new one. (Altough in the next generation of DNA, half of the helices are without any of the "grandmother" strands)The replication starts in the origins of replication (about 10,000 of them in eucaryote cells, greatly increasing the speed of replication). These replication origins are formed by specific nucleotide codes, with a majority of A-T pairs. as they form weaker (fewer) bonds than the C-G pairs, and thus require less energy to pry apart. From each of these the replication begins outwards towards both ends.At each replication origin there forms two replication forks, one at each end. As replication moves in both directions it is called bidirectional (Nor all organisms use bidirectional replication).
The replication forks are asymetrical as a resulting of the antiparallel strands of the DNA. This means that the one new strand (the leading strand) are being synthesized in the same direction (appending the 3' end) as the replication fork movement, whereas the other new strand (the lagging strand) are being synthesized away from the replication fork. However, as a result of the movement of the replication fork, this must be done discontinously (discretely) in a lot of smaller okazagi fragements, that are fused later on.
The enzymes responsible for the actual synthesis of new strands are called DNA polymerases. These catalyze the addition of nucleotides to the 3' end of a growing DNA strand, using an original strand as a template. The to-be-bound nucleotides are present as deoxyribosenucleoside triphosphates, which means that the hydrolysis of the high-energy bond, cleaving pyrophosphate (Diphosphate), fuels the forming of the phosphodiester bond it self, binding the nucleotide to the 3' end of the strand. The pyrophosphate is hydrolyzed again, making the reverse reaction very unlikely.
The DNA polymerase can't itself begin a new DNA strand, but merely add nucleotides to the growing 3' end of a strand. DNA synthesis thus requires a primer with 3'-OH (That is an exposed 3' end). This primer is RNA synthesized by DNA-primase. The DNA polymerase can then begin the DNA synthesis at the 3' end of the RNA primer On the leading strand there is only needed one primer in the beginning, from witch the DNA polymerase can synthesize the new strand continually. On the lagging strand the DNA-primase must regularly synthesize new primer, from which the DNA polymerase can backtrack, each resulting in an okazaki fragment
When the DNA polyemerase reaches the next primer in line (the next okazaki fragment) it stops Nucleases will then remove the RNA primer Repair polymerase fills out the exposed segment, until only one phosphodiester bond is missing, between each of the fragments. This bond is mended by DNA ligase fueled by ATP Firstly (in the phase) two initiator proteins Origine replication complex (ORC) and Cdc6 recognizes and binds to the origins of replication sequences Two of the proteins Helicase binds using ATP, while Cdc6 dissociates. This forms the prereplicative complex (Pre-RC) (Maybe also called the initiation complex?) When the replication is signaled the Pre-RC is activated by S-Cdk, and the replication begins. The helicase slides along the DNA disassociating the strands using ATP for energy Behind the helicase the protein monomers single-strand DNA-binding proteins (SSB) binds to the lagging string keeping it straight, and thus keeping the helix from reforming A sliding clamp is locked around each strand, by the ATP-fueled clamp loader. The polymerase is then bound to the sliding clamp, letting it slide along the strand. As the helicase dissociates the strands continuously, the leading strand-polymerase simply follows while synthesizing new DNA. On the lacking strand, a primase regularly synthesizes RNA primers, which is used by polymerase moving in the opposite direction in segments, before returning and repeating (in reality is it the strand that is moving, as the polymerase associates with the helicase complex).
During the replication there occurs supercoiling, where the DNA wraps around it self (like a cable when wrapping it around) in front of the replication, as the helicase unwraps the helix. This is solved by topoisomorase I and II. These enzymes creates a transient cleavage of the helix (one strand for topoisomerase I and the other for II), which allows the DNA to "uncoil" by rotating freely, before putting them back together
The nucleosomes dissociates, that is the histones are displaced. After the replication, the CAF1 and NAP1 recreates the now duplicated nucleosomes
When reaching the end of the DNA in a chromosome, the lead strand will finish as it should (The 3' end), but the lagging strand will finish with a RNA primer at the end (The 5' end), as there is not previous segment to reach it, and the polymerase can't synthesize DNA instead. Without a fix to this, the chromosomes wlil quicly shorten.The telomerase fixes this. At the end of the chromosome, we find a telomere repeat sequence. The telomerase extends the repeating sequence on the lead strand, such that an RNA primer can be added on complementary to this (The primer is carried and removed again by the telomerase), and the DNA polymerase can finish the lagging strand
In general the telomeres does becomes shorter with age 15000 bp from birth 7000 bp at adulthood At som point, there is no more telomerase, and the cells can no longer divide. In cancer cells, the mutations allows the telomeres to keep their length, and thus the cells becomes "immortal" Chemo therapy targets topoisomerasem which means that they can cleave the DNA, but the drugs inhibits the rebinding of the DNA, which means that the DNA is degraded and the cell dies. This is smart, because it targets cells with rapid cell division and thus DNA replication - cancer cells There are nucleotides in the human genome, which mean that a primer of length 16 can bind to one single place in the genome (). This is the principle we use in PCR.Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) A type of polymerase that can tolerate boiling, is the essence of PCR. It is a repeating three step proces: Denaturing of the DNA by heat (90 degrees) Annealing of two primers One for each end of the segment of interest (60 degrees) DNA synthesis (70 degrees)

item.description:
Tags: #CellBiology Perspectives of size a cells i between virus and sand Virus (0.1-0.5 micro m) < Cell (15 micro m) < Sand (70 mirco m) From one cell to a multicellular organism 250 types of cells 4 fundamental types of tissues Muscle tissue Nerve tissue Connective tissue (Bindevæv) Epithelial tissue The epithelial tissues can be subdivided Surface epithelial Outer Inner Glandial epithelium (Kirtelepitel) Exocrine Endoxrine Properties and functions It has some general properties that makes it unique from other cells and tissues Avascular - Meaning that it has no direct blood contact - instead they get nutrients trough the basal lamina from the connective tissues. Polarised - Apical (Fremad) / Basal (Base) Rest on the basal lamina over connective tissues Divides cells inner/outer - Keeps out patogens and antigens and resists as mechanical stress Allows directional secretion and absorption Cell contacts meaning that they are tightly packed with their neighbour They go through rapid cell division, because they are usually in vulnerable areas Cell contacts are divided into contacts between cells and contacts between extracellular matrix and cells
The important ones to know:The cell-cell contacts are divided into Occluding - Forms barriers that cant be easily passed Adhering - Gives stability and structure Communicating - Intercellular communications

Also called zonula occludens, tight junctions TJ are complete belts surrounding the cell, and not just point contacts.Transmembrane proteins - Claudine and occludine (four-pass transmembrane proteins) forms tight bonds between the cells by homophillic interactions between the extracellular domains of the proteins This keeps the cells tight Inhibits intercellular transport between the cells of aqua soluble molecules
The protein networks connects the TJ to the cytoskeleton Linking proteins (Plague protein) called Zonula Occludens (ZO-1/2/3) contains a mix of domains binding to claudin, occludin, signaling proteins, and actin - which fixes it loosly to the cytoskeleton
Functions of TJ It divedes the plasma membrine into the apical and basal (Basolaterale) domain It inhibits lateral diffusion of membrane proteins It allows polar nutrient endocytosis and exocytosis - transcytosis There can occur errors int he TJ. Claudin 1 can be defect which allows water to diffuse across the skin, which means that dehydration occurs (mice died miv) Lack of claudin 1 can lead to a lot of chronic inflammatory diseases (atopic dermatatis? check it out)
These AJ are responsible for the mechanical cobling of the cytoskeleton of neighbouring cells. This is again complete belts and not point contacts. Transmembrane cadherin The adhesion is dependent
Homophillic interactions between intracellular cadherin domains holds the membranes close. The cadherin in turn binds to plague proteins (Zonula adherens), that binds to actine filament, thus connecting it to the cytoskeleton The binding between the cadherin is dependent on the ions - these are located between the cadherins in the extracellular space
The cadherine super family of more then 180 types Allows differentiation of similar cells, which is important for different tissue types and especially neural tubes
Defects in AJ are also prevalent Defect E-cadherin in the bowels The cells cant form adherens junctions and desmosomer Disorganisted apitel with no integrity This results in an increase of pathogens and inflammatory bowels dieases The desmosomes are point contacts instead of complete belts They are very strong (Relative to the other contacts) Common in cells with great mechanical stress (Epidermis and heart muscle cells) Non-classical Cadherins – Desmoglein og desmocollin (Fine to remeber cadherins) Binds to intermediary filaments (Different types dependent on cell type) trough plague proteins
There is no actual contact at gap junctions, instead it is a gap Use for communications Channels between cell membranes The channels in the gap junction consists of two halves called connexons, each of which consists of 6 connexines Allows the passage of small molecules and ions (<1000da) 1.4 nm in diameter
The permeability of the gap junctions can be regulated by among other signal molecules.They are very common in tissues using rapid communications, such as in heart muscle cells The gap junctions (electrical synapses) allow sending action potentials across the membrane directly Allows simultaneous contractions Mutations in connexins can lead to heart faliure and heart arrhythmia (irregular heart beat) The cell-cell contacts are important for the integrity of the epithelial cells Some of these are regulated (nedreguleret) during cancer, which can result in "rogue" epethelial cancer cells, tansforming to mesenchymal cells, that is metastases The basal membrane at the base of the epethilal cells are divided into the basal lamina at the top, and reticular lamina at the bottom.the extracellular matrix is a network of Fibrose proteins - Collagens Adhesive glycoproteins - Laminin and fibronectine Proteoglycans - Perlecan, decorin, aggrecan Glycosaminglycanes (GAGs) It provides mechanical strengths and as a mechanical buffer (pillow) between cells. All cells can create the matrix, but the compostision differs between the cells. Fibroblasts - Connective tissues Osteoblasts - Skeletal ECM Chondroblasts - Cartilgae (Brusk) ECM Epithelial cells - Basal lamina ECM The basal lamina is a specialized ECM, with Adhesive glycoproteins - Laminin Collagen IV Proteoglycanes The reticular lamina consists of Collagen VII, which is in contact with the collagen IV of the basal lamina These are extracellular glycoproteins with multiple domains, that are specialised in binding to each other and other molecules, and thus creates a big network (matrix). The glycostructures are great for mechanical buffers.

Long chains of sulfating polysaccharides attached to a smaller protein There are more than 50 types, with great heterogeneity between sugars They attract water, which creates a gel-like substance They form a matrix with the glycoproteins and collagen This acts as a mechanical buffer (stødpude) while allowing diffusion of nutrients, metabolites and hormones Long proteins, the forms long fibers Creates the robe-like super-helices (triple helices) Collagen IV is characteristic for forming net like structure
The basal lamina is thus formed by the interconnections between the criss-crossing laminin, the collagen super-helices, the proteopglycanes, and some other proteins. It forms the extracellular base of the epithelial cells, between the cells and the connective tissues.
Intracellular we have keratine, plasma stif There are two kinds of Cell-ECM contacts Hemidesmosomes using intermediary filaments Focal adhesions using actin Integrines Transmembrane proteins that connects the cytoskeleton to the ECM Attach the cytoskeleton to the basal membrane They bind to the laminin if the ECM
Anchors the epithelial cells to the ECM The binds the keratine (intermediary filament) via the integrin to the adhesive glycoproteins in the ECM It is a very strong contact
The focal adhesions are cell-ECM contacts but unlike hemidesmosomes they connect with the actin of the cytoskeleton. They consists of plague proteins binding transmembrane integrins binding to fibronectines
They are quite common in fibroblast cells - see Cytoskeleton and Protein Filaments for details
Defects in the integrins can have a lot of consequences depending on the type of integrin

item.title: Oxidative Phosphorylation and Mitochondria
item.description:
Tags: #CellBiology #Energy The mitochondria is one of the few double-membrane organels of the cell. The outer membrane is covered by porin proteins making it permeable to molecules up to dalton, as well as having specific transport proteins The inner membrane hosts the electron-transport chain and the ATP synthesis. It is highly convoluted forming cristae (infolds), which increases the surface area. Its very impermeable due to the lipid cardiolipin in the membrane The matrix is the inner compartment with the mitochondrial DNA, and hundreds of enzymes for pyruvate oxidation, fatty acid oxydation, citric acid cycle and much more. This also contains the mDNA The intermembrane space contains proteins for phosphorylating nucletides (using ATP), important for the hydrogen gradient, and some pro-apoptotic factors (proteins for apoptosis) The mitochondria diffuses freely in some cells, while in others, it forms structures to supply ATP to areas of high energy consumption. In cardiac (heart) muscles, they form layers between the myofibril (contraction proteins) In sperm they surround the flagella (motor protein) In some cells they form elongated tubular networks
The mitochondria have their own mitochondrial DNA. This is 100% from the egg cell (mother), which has about 100.000 mitochondria, while the spermatoze has about 1000 mitochondria, that are marked by ubiquitin and later destroyed. (Maternal arvegang in danish) It has 16,569 nucleotide pairs 37 genes coding exclusively for the electron transport chain (making up for about 4% of the proteins in the mitochondria) The mitochondrial DNA exists in many copies, with no histones, no introns and a very simple DNA repair system. This means that every mutation in the mitochondrial DNA is expressed in some proteins. It also means, that most of the damaged mtDNA copies are destroyed (because of the damage) and thus cant be passed on Heteroplasmia is defined by having different types of mtDNA in the same tissue while homoplamsmia is defined as having the same mtDNA in all tissue. This describes both mutations and polymorphiasIt is completely random which the mitochondria is given to which cell at division, which means that we can end with some cells with mitochondrial diseases, and some without - mitochondrial segregation. This variability is called variabel expressivity
The mitochindria have more roles in the cell, than just ATP synthesis:
Simply put, the mitochondrial function can be broken down into multiple steps Citric Acid Cycle Electron Transport Chain Chemiosmosis The last two are what we call oxidative phosphorylation
The mitochondria can like whole cells split using fission. This is done using dynamine to divide the membranes (just a membrane vesicles). The mtDNA is stocastically divided, and can be uneven in numbers. We can have a too large amount of mitochondria in a given cell. These can be fused together using membrane proteins

The mitochondria in the cell is a evolutionary result of symbiosis between an early eukaryote cell and an early bacteria - curriculum is four arguments why Supported by the double membrane (One would be the bacterial membrane, and the other the endocytosis membrane) Supported by mitochondrial DNA Cardiolipin in the inner membrane - this is usually found in bacteria The ability to do fusion and fission unlike other organelles
See Compartments and Protein Distribution
In the cytosol sugars are cleaved to glucose, which is transformed to pyruvate by glycolysis: Glycolysis is important because it is a much faster reaction, than oxidative phosphorylation, which is why anaerobe respiration is faster then aerobe respiration
Pyruvate and fatty acids are translocated into the matrix, where they are converted to Acetyl CoA first (activating a little ) and then in the citric acid cycle they are oxidized to - some of the energy from which is saved in the activated carriers and . The macromolecules of food doesn't enter the mitochondria. Instead they are degregated in the cytosol and lysosomes - fats are broken down to fatty acids and polysaccharides are broken down to sugars.
Also called the respiratory chain it contains over 40 protein groups, but can be divided into three respiratory enzyme complexes (The names are not curriculum) (Complex I) NADH dehydrogenase complex - "powered" by the two high-energy electrons of the (Complex II) - Ikke i bogen - Succinate dehydrogenase is a part of the cirtus acid cyclus (Complex III) Cytochrome c reductase complex - "powered" by the high-energy ubiquinone, activated by the NADH dehydrogenase complex or through complex II (Complex IV) Cytochrome c oxidase complex - "powered" by the reduced cytochrome c
The process of transporting protons across the membrane, is possible as a result of the reduction/oxidation reactions. In aqueous environments electron carriers, that are reduced (receives an electron) often receives a from the water to balance the charge. On the other hand an electron carrier which is oxidized (looses an electron) also releases a into the water. The trick is, that the transmembrane molecules receives a proton in the water on one side of the membrane, and releases a proton to the water on the other side:
The sequence of redox-reactions of the ECT proceeds spontaneously as they have a negative . This is a result of the difference in electron affinity. Low electron affinity molecules such as NADH readily passes electrons to molecules with higher electron affinity (the NADH dehydrogenase complex).NADH is a strong electron donor (Very favorably of electron transfers) and as a result is a very weak electron donor. This is measured experimentally for redox pairs () as a redox potential (in volts). The higher the redox potential, the higher the affinity for electrons - that is redox pairs with low potential, transfer their electrons to redox pairs with high potential.
The difference in redox potential is a direct measure of , and thus the describes how energetically favorable the electron transfer actually is. (, where is the number of electrons transferred per mV change in redox potential)If the NADH transferred the electrons directly to the would be so huge, that a ton of energy would be released as heat. By splitting the reaction into multiple transfers and thus pumping many protons across the membrane, we utilize as much as the free energy as possible.
Each of the complexes utilizes metals with different electron affinities, which allows a donated electron to skip between embedded metal ions within the complex. When transferring between complexes, the electrons are passed to electron carries that can diffuse freely in the lipid bilayer. The iron-sulfur centers have low affinity and are present in the NADH dehydrogenase complex The iron in a heme group have somewhat higher affinity and are present in both cytochrome c reductase, cytochrome c oxidase and cytochrome c itself. The slight difference in structure and amino acid environment determines the electron affinity of the ions, and thus can a "staircase" along the complex be built. The energy from the electron transport are though to bring the complexes into a conformation where affinity goes from high to low, and can be released in the inner membrane side
The ubiquinone is a molecule with a long hydrophobic tail and a carbon ring, that can accept two electron (and protons). This picks up electrons from the NADH dehydrogenase complex, and delivers them to the cytochrome c reductase complex. It can also accept electrons directly from generated in the citric cycle and fatty acid oxidation
The cytochrome c is another electron carrier, that accepts four electrons from the cytochrome c reductase (hence the name), moves along the membrane in the inner membrane space (not in the lipid bilayer), and transfers them to the cytochrome c oxidase (hence the name).
The cytochrome c oxidase is where the is reduced. It has the highest electron affinity in the chain. An oxygen binding site contains a heme group and a copper atom. Here four electrons (and protons) are transferred to resulting in while four other protons are pumped across the membrane. Toxins such as cyanide is highly dangerous because it binds tightly to the cytochrome c oxidase halting the electron transport.The electrochemical gradient of across the inner membrane, which is created by the elctron transport chain, drives the synthesis of ATP from and . This synthesis is facilitated by ATP synthase. It consist of A stationary head (of multiple subunits) called ATPase head The is kept stationary by the peripheral stalk - a transmembrane protein A rotating part (of multiple subunits) called rotor - A transmembrane rotate-able carrier (Rotor ring) attached to a central stalk The rotor is driven by the proton influx, which in turn rotates the central stalk inside the . This changes the conformation of the head - driving the synthesis of from + .
The proces of the ATP synthase is reversible, meaning that if the electrochemical gradient of falls below a certain level - it will instead perform ATP hydrolysis to drive the rotor, transporting out of the membrane. The reversal point is when the energy - required to synthezise ATP (Which is of course dependent on the concentrations of ATP and ADP) is just equal to the energy delivered by the proton transportThe proton gradient does not only facilitate the synthesis of ATP, but also other processes. Carrier proteins transports pyruvate, ADP, into the matrix and ATP out of it. This is agains their concentration gradients, and thus requires energy. This is done through coupled transport (Both antiporters and symporters) with the proton influx. Other antiporters utilize the membrane potential created by the electron transport chain to transport (charged) out of the cell and into the cell.
Also for protein translocation into the mitochondria (somehow? Protein distribution) It can have direct functional properties such as in bacteria, where the influx of protons drive the rapid rotation of the flagellum
The cell needs to keep about 10:1 ratio of ATP:ADP in order to drive the energetically unfavorable reactions, that enzymes catalyze by coupling them to ATP hydrolysis.The pumping per complex: Complex I - Pumps 4 Complex II - Pumps no Complex III - Pumps 4 Complex IV - Pumps 2 And because the ATP synthase synthesises one ATP per 2.7 we have: When looking at the production values of each process in terms of ATP, we see a highly effective machine of energy-transformation. NADH provides net energy to generate about 2.5 ATP in the ETC provides 1.5 ATP in the ETC GDP = ADP in as thay have the same high-energy phosphate bond We can thus calculate the total energy of the subprocesses:Yielding in a total of 30 ATP, which is of the total energy that would be released when burning the sugar. In comparison a motor (Electric or gasoline) opperates at about 10-20% efficiency. - This is freaking awesome by the way

item.title: Compartments and Protein Distribution
item.description:
Tags: #CellBiology In order for the cell to keep an organization of the different metabolic pathways, it needs to keeps them somewhat separate. This is done by compartmentalizing the cell, creating the membrane-covered organnels. Thus proteins can be sorted to their respective places by sorting mechanism. Membranes play a role in much more than the plasma membrane. Membrane-divided compartments include Mitochondria Endoplasmatic Reticulum - Smooth and rough Golgi apparatur Nucleus Lysosomes Peroxisomes Endosomes Vesicles of all kinds The plasma membrane make up for of the lipid bilayer in most cells:
All of these different compartments have different functions, needs different proteins, and are a part of different pathways.In order to distribute the proteins between these compartments, the cell needs methods to differentiate and later transport each protein to the correct place across the membrane.Specific sequences of amino acids works as a sort of postal addres in the cell. These are called signal sequences. They are independent of the protein function, and can be freely moved to other proteins (e.g. using crisper) while retaining the function for transport.
The three general distribution systems: In vesicles - The secretory pathway Across membranes directly using translocation proteins + receptors (ER, Mitochondria, and Peroxisomes) Through pores in the double membrane of the nucleus
The DNA has 19670 genes coding for proteins, of which 36% () are sorted by the secretory pathway. The secretory pathway describes the ER system with Co-translational translocation of proteins into the ER lumen Protein modifications in the ER Transport to the Golgi apparaturs Protein modifications in the Golgi apparatus and intra Golgi transport (From Cis-golgi to Trans-golgi (TGN)) Transport from the Golgi apparatus To the plasma membrane (Exocytosis) with constitutive secretion To secretary granules (vesicles) for regulated secretion To lysosomes in the form of vesicles forming early endosomes or fusing with late endosomes / lysosomes (Endolysosomal system)
This is a method used to transport the proteins across the membranes of the rough ER simultaneously as the translation takes place A free ribosome starts translating the mRNA sequence The terminus of the peptide chain forms a specific signal sequence, which is recognized by a signal recognitions particle (SRP) - this slows the synthesis This SRP then binds to an SRP receptor, which then connects the ribosome complex to a protein translocator or translocon This binds the signal sequence and the SRP is displaced for later use The synthesis resumes which simultaniously "pushes" the peptide chain through the receptor, into the ER Lumen. The signal peptide is cleaved from the protein by signal peptidase
The translocon in the rough ER is called Sec61, and it that has two important parts: A plug that blocks transport across the pore. This is displaced by the signal sequence, allowing translocation of the peptide chain. A latteral gate which can open a "door" to the membrane, allowing for a transmembrane protein to be released into the lipid bilayer - or for soluble proteins, it releases the signal peptide Not only singlepass transmembrane proteins can be released into the membrane. The poly-peptide sequence can code for start-transfer and stop-transfer sequences, both of which code for a transmembranial parts of the multipass protein:


In the lumen of the ER, the proteins can undergo multiple modifications Folding and multimerization - That is, the polypeptide chain must gain its secondary, tertiary and quarternary structure GPI-anchoring where a transmembrane protein is cleaved at the C-terminal (Transmembrane part), which is repalced by a glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) - a membrane lipid covalently linked to a carbohydrate (phostphate). This called a GPI anchor.
The oxidation of disulfide bridges between the cysteine in the folded proteins. This is catalyzes by an oxidized protein disulfide isomerase (PDI), which binds to the cysteine, reduced, and the protein is oxidized.
N-glycosylation, which is where oligosaccharides are transfered en block from a lipid precurser to the amide of asparagin. This is catalyzed by oligosaccharyltransferase (OST) It gives the protein properties of shape, size and polarity. It helps with the correct folding - quality control
After glycosylation the oligosaccharide is trimmed by Glucosidase I which removes the outermost glucose. Glucosidase II which removes the next two glucose residues, leaving a monoglucosylated glycan Proteolytic activation - that is the cleavage of proproteins as a part of the maturity (Cleavage of signal peptide e.g.) There is also systems in the lumen of the ER to ensure proper folding. Multiple chaperones act upon the newly synthesized protein: BiP Chaperones binds to the polypeptide chain to avoid premature misfolding just after synthesis Lectins, which binds to monoglucosylated glycoproteins (after N-glycosylation and glucosidase I and II trimming), perform the same role of assisting in folding Calnexin (CNX) - A membrane-bound chaperone Calreticulin (CRT) - A soluble chaperone Glucosidase II removes the last glucose, which releases the proteins form the lectins If the folding is correct, the proteins go on - but if it is misfolded the protein is re-glycosylated by GDDP, which means, that the lectins can bind again, to retry folding If the re-glycosylation fails, another system for folding is Endoplasmic Reticulum Associated Degradation (ERAD) The misfolded protein is translocated out of the lumen, where it is bound to ubiquitin by the enzyme ubiquitin ligase They are recognized by the proteasome, which degrades the protein such that it doesn't accumulate, and such that it can be up-cycled
When a lot of misfolded proteins accumulate in the ER this sends an unfolded protein response (URP). This can result in multiple things: More chaperones are synthesized and added to assist in the folding of the proteins Send a signal to stop the transcription of the misfolded accumulated protein In the worst case it will send signals to start apoptosis The (smooth) ER also has a function of synthesizing new lipids and as a storage of molecules such as . The principles of vesicle transport is a part of a compartment, which include soluble and membrane cargo molecules,
The cytosol side of the membrane creates vesicles by budding, while becoming covered in a COPII coat. These are grouped in a vesicular tubular cluster, which can be recognized and moved along the microtubuli by the power of motor proteins.Some proteins are sent in the opposite directions (retrieval transport), the vesicles are coated in a COPI coat - This is often proteins (usually chaperone proteins) that are sent to golgi by mistake (that is they have a retention signal)

Inside the golgi apparatus, more protein modifications take place. The golgi consist of a stack of folded compartments called cisternae - each golgi stack hacing between 3 and 20 cisterna (and cells having 1 to 100s of stacks). Each stack has a cis face towards the ER and a trans face away from the ER. Cis Golgi Network (CGN) Soluble proteins and membrane proteins enter the CGN via vesicles from the ER. Some of these contains ER-retention signals and are sent back instead of moving on in the golgi. Here the oligosoccharides on lysosomal proteins are phosphorylized - this is called a Monose-6-phosphate M6P tag, which is signal for sending it on to the lysosomes We see O-glycosylation where GalNAc-transferases adds GalNAc to the hydroxyl group of serine/threonine (Cis/Medial/Trans) Cisternea N-Glycosylation continues (Trimming Mannose), where mannosidases removes sugars from high-mannose N-glycans GlcNAc-transferases add GlcNAc to trimmed glycans. Sulfotransferases add sulfate (SO₄) to tyrosine or glycans Trans Golgi Network (TGN) Kinaser phosphorylate serine/threonine/tyrosine on proteins. Furin, PC1/3, PC2 cut proproteins to activate them
In the TGN the proteins are sorted by constitutive secretion or regulated secretion.Constitutive secretion means the the vesicles are uncoated and delivered directly to the membrane, where they are released by exocytosis. This is for example: Collagen, fibronectine, ion channels and receptors Regulated secretion means that the vesicles are coated by clathrine until they are matured, at which point the clathrine is returned and they form secretory granules These are ready to be used in the given pathway (neurotransmitters, amylase, histamine, insulin, etc.). This includes proprotein processing - e.g. insulin which exists in the trans-golgi network as proinsulin, which is split to insulin and a C-peptide. For both regulated and constitutive secretion, the exicytosis happens by fusion with the membrane Tethering - Rab-GTP transports the vesicle to the membrane, where if tetheres to **tethering proteins. Docking - the v-SNARE on the vesicles form a complex with the t-SNARE on the membrane, Fusion - a twirl of the complex pushed the membranes together until they fuse
There are multiple types of endocytosis Pinocytosis where fluid and small molecules (vesicles <150 nm diameter) Spontaneous process Non-specialized - all cells do it Phagocytosis where larger particles with vesicles > 250 nm This is only specialized cells such as in the immune system, where they can perform phagocytosis on bacteria Receptor-mediated endocytosis which is when clathrin coated pits on the extracellular side of the membrane is budded into the cell. E.g. LDL particles from the blood stream Autophagi which is the degradation of the cells own organelles The organelle is surrounded by a membrane (somehow?) and transfered to the lysosomes where it merges Technically not endocytosis, but often mentioned together

Lipids and cholesterols are transported in the blood by large low-density lipoproteins (LDL), which is recognized by LDL-receptors and tranlocated into the cell by endocytosis. This is fused with the endosome, where the receptor is released into a vesicle and exocytosis - this is an example of Receptor-mediated endocytosis Carge receptors recognize the cargo molecules, and binds intracellularly to adaptine 1 (adaptine 2 is used for transport from glogi to endosomes) These are coated by clathrine and forms a bud The bud is released by dynamin and a clathrine coated vesicle is formed The calthrine-adaptin complexes release the receptors, and the transport vesicle is uncoated After excocytosis, the LDL-vesicles are sent to an endosome Here the acidic environment unbinds the LDL from the receptors The LDL-receptors are sent back to the plasma membrane in a vesicle called recycling Other proteins can be sent to another location on the plasma membrane (important for epithel cells with tight junctions) - this is called transcytosis The LDL is passed on to the lysosomes to be degraded The coats involved in the secretory pathway:
Some proteins are destined for the processes of degregation in the lysosomes. These proteins have a signal patch consisting of the phosphorylized oligosaccharides called M6P. This is recognized by M6P receptors in the trans-golgi network, and are sent from the golgi in vesicles coated by adaptine 1 and clathrine. After delivery, the M6P receptors are send back to the golgi in retromer coated vesicles.The lysosome in it self as the cells degradation centers There exists multiple pathways to the lysosomes. Small (0.2 - 0.5 ) spherical membrane structures Proton pumps keep the pH at 4.5-5.0 The have hydrolytic enzymes which are at their acidic optimum at the lysosomal pH. There is a lot of lysosomal storage disease as a result of different dysfunctional hydrolytic enzymes
Small molecules (5000 Da to 60 kDa) can pass the nucleus pores by simple diffusion.The nuclear proteins are synthesizes in the cytosol. When the NLS sequence is exposed, they are bound to the nuclear import receptors. This receptor transports the protein complex into the nuclear pore, where they can step-wise bind to the nuclear pore proteins, that otherwise form a gel-like substance.
Inside nucleus, the Ran-GTP will swap place with the protein complex, and receptor moves out of the pore again, where the Ran-GTP is hydrolized by Ran-GAP, and thus releases the receptor. Thus the import process can repeat. The Ran-GDP is phophorylized by RAN-GEF in the nucleus.
While the mitochondria have DNA coding for some proteins, most of the are imported from the cytosol. The precursor protein (with the signal peptide) is recognized by import receptor proteins called importion, which is binds to the translocator in the outer membrane (TOM) This complex moves to a narrow membrane segment, where it can bind to an inner membrane translocator (TIM). Here the protein unfolds and translocates into the matrix, where the signal peptide is cleaved and the protein is matured - This translocation and folding process is facilitated by chaperone proteins which uses ATP for the proces. Once the signal peptide is cleaved, further signals may be decoded from the chain - for example for the transport to the inner membrane or the matrix.

The peroxisomes receives proteins both as vesicle transport from the ER (or golgi), and directly from the cytosol. The translocation proteins of the peroxides are special, as they can translocate the proteins without unfolding them.
