item.title: Cytoskeleton and Protein Filaments
item.description:
Tags: #CellBiology The cytoskeleton gives the cell form and mobility. It consists of the three classes of filaments Actine (diam. 7 nm) Intermediaru (diam. 10 nm) Microtubili (diam. 25 nm)
They are formed by -helical peptide chains forming coiled-coil dimers, these are staggered to form tetramers, which can be packed head to head in "layers" of eight This means that they are not polar
This rope-like structure gives them tensile strength - that is ability to take tension without breaking. Except for lamin, which exist in all nuclei of animal cells, the peptides are specific for each tissue-type Keratin filaments play an important role in epthelial cells

Desmosomes are the contact point between intermediary filaments of neighbouring cells. (See Cell-Cell and Cell-ECM Contact)
Actine have a variety of functions, but generally it is associated with the movements of the cell - especially those related to the membrane. But also structure and intercellular contact (Tight junctions).
Many of the functions are done with the help of actin-binding proteins. Some of which include: Nucleating protein Monomer-sequestering protein Severing protein - for breaking filaments into smaller parts Bundling proteins Myosin motor proteins - Different types! Capping proteins Cross-linking proteins
Actin filament is on its own (no actin-binding proteins) an unstable structure, that can assemble and disassemble spontaneously. The actine monomers are called G-actine. It is a polar molecules meaning, that the direction matters, and it will always bind its minus-end, to the exposed plus-end in the sequence, called the F-actine.The G-actine comes together in a polar filament with a coupled ATP. Shortly after incorporation however, the ATP is hydrolyzed, and the binding is not as strong. Thus the ADP-actin dissociates in the minus end (if no protein stop it). This means that the f-actin grows and shrinks, depending of the rates polymerization and depolymerization. When these are equal, we say that the actin is treadmilling. This if course is a somewhat waste of energy, but it is the price to pay for The critical concentration of G-actine - is the tipping point for polymerization and depolymerization: : Depolymerazation : Polymerization
Some proteins can catalyze the synthesis of F-actine. Formins cap the minus end Spires ARP2/3 complex
The actin is responsible for cell surface specializations such as microvilli found on the apical surface of some epithelial cells.
It also plays a role in holding the plasma membrane in shape via the cortex, and the structure of adhesion belts in epithelial cells.F-actine affects not just the structure, but also the dynamics of the plasma membrane and the cell it self.Some bacteria can push forward by polymerization of tail f-actines - called actin filament comet
Cell migration is movement of the human cells caused by actine
The actine creates lamellipodium by pushing the plasmamembrane. Filopodia are stiff thin protrutions, which are produced simmilarly - this is how the axon of the neurons are produced. The actin polymerization begins by EGF signalling This activates cofilin - severing the capped end of the f-actine by the membrane - exposing the plus end Thus the polymerization begins of the exposed plus ends (ATP F-actin caps) Arp2/3 fascilitates dendritic nucleation, that is the branching of the actine to cover more area forming lamellipodium Formin promotes the polymerization of long straigth filaments forming filopedia
When in the new region, the filopedia of the leading edge of the lamellipodium and the lamellipodium it self then adhere to molecules in the extracellular matrix or on the neighboring cell surface via integrins in the plasma membrane of the migrating cell. The cell then contracts by myosin-1 sliding the stress fibers forward in the "end" of the cell - pulling the back of the cell body forward
Myosin works together with f-actine to create movement Myosin 1 - motor proteins that can transport cargo along the filmanet Myosin 2 - the proteins responsible for muscle cell contration Myosin 1 has a single globular head domain, that binds to actin filament and hydrolyzes ATP to allow directional movement. - The actual movement dynamic is a bit unclear They can transport cargo along actine filaments They can be bound to plasma membrane, and thus pull the cell along the actin. It moves unidirectionally towards to plus end of the filament
Actine regulation - The f-actine in the cytoskeleton is controlled by GTPaser An examples is: VEGF binds to VEGF-receptor extracellularly The GTPase Rac1 is activated This activatres the kinase PAK Which activates the kinase LIMK This inhibits cofilin, which means that the ADP-actin filament is not severed, and the network will stabilize (decrease new polymerization) This is because the severing of ADP-actin filaments will stimulate new polymerizations. Actin also plays an important role in the mitosis, that is the cytokinesis. Here actin creates a contractile ring including: tropomyosin myosin II formin crosslinking proteins This ring will tighten and "pinch" the cell in two. (The last part is carried out by ESCRT-III complex)
A lot of toxins have an effect on actine Phalloidine Cytochalasine Latrunculine Microtubi are organised from the microtubli organization center (MTOC), which is either centrosomes or basal bodiesFormed by dimer of -tubulin and -tubilin Polar with -tubilin in the plus end and -tubilin in the minus end They form long a cylinder of 13 protofilaments in a ring
Most microtubilu extend from centrosomes. These constists of a pair of centrioles (consisting of short microubili fibers) and protein complex with -tubilin rings, which are perfect starting points for forming microtubili, as the energy requirement for spontaneous cyllinders forming is too big. They grow their plus ends outwards from the -tubulin rings
Dynamic instability Like actine - we use energy by bindig tubuline dimers with GTP. This GTP is hydrolyzed once part of the microubuli. When phosphorylzed, the dimers binds strongly, whereas dephosphorylized dimers binds weakly, and will tear away from the microtobuli, if exposed to an open plus end. Thus when the addition of dimers is faster than the hydrolyzis, the microtubuli grows - Elongation If it is slower, the dimers peel away - Rapid shortening
Each of these microtubili spontaneously grows and shrinks independent of each other, sometimes disappearing completely, until the plus end finds some capping protein (or are associated with other proteions), in which case it is stable.Microtubuli form the cilia on the epithel cells. These hairlike structure extends from the basal body. These consists of two central microtubuli surrounded by nine pair of microtubuli and some structural proteins.
Most importantly though, is the motor protein ciliary dynein (Different from transport dynein). These motor proteins slides the pairs of microtubulis away from each other. Linking proteins keeps the slide from being even, and instead by tension, creates the bending of the cilia.
Cellular transport the polarity of the microtubuli makes both anterograde and retrograde transport possible (Anterograde transport means away from the MCOT / soma) The motor protein dynein transports cargo retrograde Attachment proteins determine cargo type The motor protein kinesen (related to myosin) It can have attachment proteins, but doesn't always
The directional movement along the microtubuli is called saltatory movement. Both protein have many conformations, that if left at random, would make them "walk" back and forth in no direction on average, what we call brownian movement or random walk. By using energy from ATP-hydrolysis to drive the series of conformations, they form directional movement. They do vary somewhat in the mechanism: The conformational changes of kinesin makes it "walk" along the fiber, putting one globular head in front of the other again and again. The conformation changes of dynein makes it "inch" along the fiber, moving the heads small steps, without flipping each step.

The transport along the micro tubuli in the axons illustrate the velocity of transports. The anterograde transport can vary in speed depending on transport, but as fast as 400 mm/day. This could be synaptic vesicles, enzymes and neurotransmitters (200-400 mm/day) Mitochondria (50-100 mm/day) Slow transport with Slow Component a (SCa) (0.1 - 1 mm/day) and Slow Component b (SCb) (2-6 mm/day) - Cytoskeleton proteins, clathrines, and cytoplasmic enzymes The retrograde transport is more constant in speed at 100-200 mm/day. Prelysosomal vesicles, recycled proteins, neurothropic viruses, etc. The ER is attached to kinesine which pulls it outwards into the cytoplasm, while the golgi is attached to dynein pulling it towards the nucleus (and the ER)
The microtubuli doesn't reach the membrane, so in order to go all the way, the actine filaments must also be used for transport The kinsesin can pass along its cargo from microtubili transport to actine transport by binding it to actine motor proteins and releasing it it self. By affecting (restricting / boosting) polymerization of micrutobili, we can combat cell division and thus cancer:
The different filaments have features, that gives them different strengths The graph visualizes the stress (Pulling force) on different filaments of the cytoskeleton, showing their percentwise elongation (strain) and breaking point Microtubules ruptures easily after and 80% increase in length F-actin ruptures after somewhat more pressure, but not much elongation Vimentin (Intermediary filament) streches a lot, but remains undamaged under high stress (Fibrin not relevant)
The protein plectin plays an important role in connecting the filaments of the cytoskeleton. It binds to each of the three filament types, and other plectines, to creating junctions of filaments. It also plays a role in the membrane junctions, where cell-cell- contacts take place.

Recepter cells are biological transducers that can convert energy from different types of physical energy frem sensory stimuli, to electrical energy of membrane- and actionpotential.After origin of stimuli Exteroceptors - Register stimuli on the organism surface (Touch, taste, heat, etc.) Interoception - Registor internal stimuli (Blood pressure, and ) Proprioception - The position and movement of body parts (Motor system and efferent copies) After the adequte stimuli for the sensory receptors Photoreceptors - reacts to lights (Sight) Kemoreceptors - reacts to chemicals (Taste, smells) Mechanocepters - reacts to mechanical deformation (Touch, sound) Termoceptors - reacts to temperature Nociceptors - reacts to tissue damage and trauma (Pain) Afsender versus modtagerdel? The sensory cells can be separate from the transmission (afsender) part Primary sensory receptors receives the stimulus energy, which activates an action potential, transmittet to the CNS through the afferent axon Secundary sensory receptors receives the stimulis energy, which released tranmitters to another cell, where action potentials are generated and transmitted to the CNS Sensory strength?


Curriculumm for signaling cascase Merkel cells Srtech receptors in grasshopper wings Photo receptor The merkel cells are located between ... They can detect strech in the skin It is a secondary sensory receptor The more strech, that higher the action potential frequence The adaptation of the strech receptor is mostly phasic but also tonic
Cones and Rods The cell is depolarized until exposed to photons Light hits the rhodopsin Activating G-protein Catalyzing the synthesis of cGMP ... 1 light quant = -1mV in the membrane potential The afferent axon can transmit signals between 3 Hz and 300 Hz
The dynamic area is the stimulus-strength interval, where to different stimulus strength will result in two different impulse frequencies. If this interval was two large, we would not be able to differentiate between small stimulis strength differences. Instead the area is dynamic, meaning that at can be small enough for us to differentiate small changes (when in the right area), while being moveable to fit the average stimuli at a given moment - adaptation. channels in the transmitter part decreases the frequency of APs, making the registration og larger sensory stimuli possible - They define the width of the interval. The channels are closed and inactivated at the resting potential When the cell as hyperpolarized, they open When the cell depolarizes (New AP) they are inactivated
channels also exists in other neurons than sensory receptors.There is tonic and phasic adaptation Different sensory cells different adaptation
The tonic receptors adapts slowly to change the dynamic area to the average stimulis strength This however means, that some stimuli are outside of the dynamic areas, and you are "blind" until adaptation
The tonic receptors are slowly adapting, meaning, that they register the stimulus strength (or rather the stimulus change , as the adaptation of the dynamic areas, means that the absolut stimuli strength can't be know) The dynamic area doesn't shift by small variations in the stimuli close to the average It does however change, when the average shifts (E.g. stepping into a dark room, from the outside) This when "understimulating" we experience an interval with no activity before the adaptation catches up - the Post Excitatory Pause (PEP) The phasic receptors detect the temporal dynamics of stimuli change
The dynamic area adapts almost as fast as the stimuli, meaning that the frequency of the APs reflect how fast the change og stimuli strength happens, that is they detect This means that phasic receptors don't registrate constant stimuli, as Many receptors both somewhat phasic and somewhat tonic, meaning that they are sensitive to and - these are called tonic-phasic receptorsThe adaptation happens as a part of every proces - Absorption, Transduction, Transformation and outside of the receptorOutside of the receptor (Before the receptor) Anatomical changes - e.g. pupils regulates the light on the retina The changes the receptor potential During the absorption/transduction Deregulation of the receptor (e.g. rhodopsin) or the transduction mechanism as a result of stimulation This changes the receptor potential During the transformation The depolarization opens the channels and depolarizes the cell Voltage gated channels opens at each AP The is removed gradually, but not fast enough channels open proporitonal to the amount of These prolong the refractory period and the frequence of APs decrease This continues until the is in equilibrium (As the frequency of APs increase, less enters the cell, while the efflux is constant) This does not change the receptor potential

item.title: Synaptic Transmission (NeuroFys)
item.description:
Tags: #Neuroscience #CellBiology Every neuron forms between 1000 and 10000 synapses to other nerves. Given we have synapses (Hundrede millioner millioner)There is multiples locations of synapses between neurons Axo-dendritic synapses on the dendrite (dendritic spines mostely) Axo-somatic synapses directly on the soma/pekaryon Axo-axonic synapses are often times synapses near axon terminal of another neuron (modulating the next synapse for example) There are two types of synapses Electrical synapses - When current flows directly between the neurons Chemical synapses - When presynaptic neurons release vesicles of transmitters in the synaptic cleft In the electrical synapsis, the presynaptic and postsynaptic neuron are connected by a gap junction. The channels in the gap junction consists of two halves called connexons, each of which consists of 6 connexines
They are really fast - with an delay of 0.2 to 0.5 ms They are bi-directional, meaning that an action potential can deliver current and thus depolarize in both directions They retain the "charge" of the transmission (If the presynaptic transmission is positive then the postsynaptic potential is positive and vice versa) They can control their effect size by opening/closing the gap junctions They work in synchronization mostly, meaning that the almost all actions potentials in the presynaptic neuron creates an action potential in the postsynaptic current Often time, the electrical synapses is not between axon terminal and densrite, but instead they are located between somas of different neurons
For the chemical synapses we can look ath the pre-synaptic mechanisms, the post-synaptic mechanisms, and the synaptic cleftWhat we see in the microscope is the axon terminal with a lot of vesicles and the active zone, where the calcium channels and vesicle exocytosis takes place, in the presynaptic cell, and the postsynaptic density where the receptors are placed.
Chemical synapses have a number of qualities They are "slow" with a delay ms They are unidirectional They can reverse the signal (or not) They are very plastic There are quite a portion of membrane proteins facilitating the functions of the transmitter vesicles. Some of the most important are Synaptobrevin also called v-SNARE, which is part of the SNARE-complex when the vesicle is primed Synaptagmine-1 (Syt1) acts as the binding site Rab3 plays a role in binding to RIM, keeping the synaptotagmine-1 close to the -channels V-ATPase is important for pumping out of the vesicles. This is used creating a electrochemical gradient for transporting neurotransmitters into the vesicle by symport
Vesicles can be in three states: Freely diffusing vesicles (not ready for exocytosis) (98%-99% of vesicles) Tethered / Docked vesicles - in the active zone, but not primed for fusion yet Primed vesicles - Activated, waiting for fusion, by signalling Only 1-2% of vesicles are primed - These are called the Readily Realsable Pool.When docked: The Rab3 on the vesicles tethers to the RIM, which binds to RIM-BP and the -channels This keeps the synaptotagmin close to the site af influx. Unc13 binds to t-snares SNAP-25 and Syntaxin-1, while tethering to synaptobrevin, thus pulling the vesicle to the release site. When being primed: Munc18 replaces unc13 The SNARE-complex forms by synaptobrevin "curling/zipping" together with syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25 Complexin in the SNARE-complex blocks fusion of the membranes
The synaptotagmine has two binding sites for called c-domains, and when they bind (From lecture) the positivity of the ions, allows the negative membranes of the vesicle and plasma membrane to get close and fuse (From book) the complexin is displaced, allowing the SNARE-complex to "zip" As a result of both, the membranes fuse, and the neurotransmitters are released into the synaptic cleft. The influx of is very transient ( 0.5 ms), meaning that it is a very local domain of high . The nano domain of a single channel is why the protein-structures keep the synaptotagmin close to the channel, so that it can be activated across 20-50 nm. Multiple channels can create a micro domain, with longer diffusion time, which begins the fusion of multiple vesicles over a longer time scale and delay After fusion, the SNARE-complex must be pulled apart. N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive fusion protein (NSF) binds to the SNARE-complex, which disassembles it with the energy delivered by ATP-hydrolysis SNAP-25 and syntaxin remains in the plasma membrane Synaptobrevin returns to synaptic vesicles by endocytosis (different mechanisms) The name SNARE comes from Soluble NSF-Attachment protein Receptor
After release of NTs into the synaptic cleft, they are either ... Kiss-and-run (We dont believe that?) - Fast (10-20s) This involves a transient fusion followed by immediate closing of the pore and endocytosis, such that the proteins of the vesicles doesn-t mix with the plasma membrane proteins Endosomal recycling - Slow (About 1 min) Bulk membrane forms large endosomal vesicales, which can be "cleaned" before forming new synaptic vesicles Clathrin-mediated endocytosis Here the synaptic vesicles completely collapses with the plasma membrane, followed by clathrin-mediated endocytosis Clathrin-Independent endocytosis (ingen eksamensspørgsmål) (100ms) Endocytic vesicles larger than synaptic vesicles are produces next to the active zone, which "swallows" everything, fusing with synaptic endosomes, where normal clathrin-mediated vesicles forming happens Receptors of the postsynaptic side are divided into Ionotropic receptors which opens an ion channels directly (A few miliseconds) Metabotrobe receptors are indirect receptors, that can have a multitude of effects - but some open ion channels, just must slower than the ionotropic receptors (100 ms to minutes)
Some neurotransmitters can activate certain types of both receptors, while others are unique ot one of the receptor types. (See Neurotransmitters and Recptors) The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor (nAChRs) is a good example of an ionotropic receptor. It is present int he neuromuscular junction (NMJ) where the motor neurons form synapses on the muscle fiber. The postsynaptic part in the NMJ is called the motor end plate.The nAChR has five subunits, where at least two are -subunits. The binding of two acetylcholine results in a conformational change, which makes the pore permeable to both and .
The acetylcholine is only present shortly in the synaptic cleft, as the enzyme acetylcholinesterase is quick to degrade the acetylcholine into acetat and choline, which is transportet into the presynaptic cell by symporters. A lot can go wrong in this process Toxins can block the nAChRs causing paralysis and asphyxiation curare - Paralyzing agent used by indegenous tribes in south america (blowing pipes) -bungarotoxin - Venom of the many-braided krait (snake) Toxins can activate the nAChRs Nicotine (giving name to the receptor) Diseases include Lambert Eaton Myastehnic Syndrom - The presynaptic -channels of NMJs are reduced, resulting in muscular weakness Myasthenia gravis - Disease where antibodies target nAChRs and thus weaknings the synapses Toxins can block the acethylcholinesterase - Used both for medicin and poison Sarin and VX - Both are nerve gasses that kills you quickly by asphyxiation, as the muscles (including the diaphragm) becomes unsuable Malathion - Insectiside Neostigmine - Medicine for opposing blockers of acethylcholine (Agains myasthenia gravis) What is a neurotransmitter? Three critera: It exists in neurons It is released as a result of an action potential It activates a receptor in the post synaptic cell They can be classified in three groups (Which is a bit weird, as the neurotransmitter is only as excitatory and inhibitory as its receptor, and the same neurotransmitter can have different functions in different synapses) Excitatory neurotransmitters - Glutamate, acetylcholin (in muscles), serotinine (sometimes) Inhibitory neurotransmitters - GABA (In cortex and cerebellum) , glycin (in the brain stem and spine) Modulatory neurotransmitters (Metabotrobe receptors) - Noradrenalin, dopamine, serotonin, histamine, acetylcholin (in CNS) The neurons can also release peptide chains called neuropeptides, which can have properties of a neurotransmitter.Each channel has a reversal potential, that is dependent on the ion concentrations extracellular and intracellular. For receptors permeable to only one ion, the reversal potential is equal to the equilibrium potential for that ion.Som channels are permeable to multiple ions (E.g. AMPA is permeable to both and ). This mean that the reversal potential is equal somewhere between the two equilibrium potentials. (For AMPA it is about 0 mV). The current of a channels is dependent on the memrabane potential and the reversal potential.A transmission is exitatory (stimulating) if it increases the probability of the postsynaptic cell firing (EPSP). This is for example the glutamate receptors, and the nAch receptors, both of which are permeable to both and . Beacause it is permeable to both, the reversal potential must be higher than the threshold of the action potential
A transmission is inhibitory if it decreases the probability of the postsynaptic cell firing (IPSP). This is for example the receptor and the glycine receptor. These are permeable to . The synapses are inhibitory, because the reversal potential is lower than the membrane potential - and thus hyperpolarizing the cell.Sometimes an inhibitory transmission can become exhibitory. If the intracellular concentration of is higher, it can result i the reversal potential of the and glycine receptors to become: Equal to the membrane potential (), which is called shunting inhibition Higher than the threshold, which means, that they are excitatory - This is the case for neurons very early in development (Embryonal)
The potential change from a single EPSP is rarely enough the reach the threshold, and thus multiple synaptic transmissions must be received (both spatially and temporally). Most excitatory synapses are located at the dendritic spines and presynaptic terminals, whereas inhibitory synapses are located on dendritic shafts, the soma and axon initial segments (as well as the dendritic spines and presynaptic terminals), making the able to stop the spread of the EPSP via shunting inhibition. Modulatory synapses can form all over. There is also a factor of distance, as the magnitude of the potential change declines with distance (Length constant - ). Here the shunting inhibition also has an effect, as is "shunts" the EPSP, which can be described as lowering the length constant. The two combined effects: Hyper-polarization of the membrane potential decreases the added effect of the EPSP and IPSP Shunting allows current to "leak" across the membrane, decreasing the amplitude of the EPSP it self
In reality this is a large calculation of multiple EPSPs, IPSPs and shunting inhibitions separated in both time and space
Bernard Katz showed that postsynaptic cell (muscle) showed small spikes called miniature EndPlatePotential (mEPP), each of which is the receival of one discrete package or quant of neurotransmitters, which we now know is one vesicle. Each vesicle is of a certain size and thus have a fixed amount of neurotransmitters He also showed by fitting the number of mEPP to the binomial distribution, that the release of quants are stochastic for an action potential.
This also means, that not all action potentials deliver neurotransmitters, and as the channels also are stochastic (they have a probability of activating at a certain voltage), a lot of stochastic activity is integrated in the neuron.
But how does synapses work reliably of they are stochastic? Have many of them! The axon can branch and form many parallel synapses with active zones of the same postsynaptic cell - e.g. the motor neurons forming many NMJ on the muscle fiber:
Multiple proteins are used for structuring the synaptic cleft. Neuroxin 1 creates a bridge from the presynaptic cell to the neuroligin in the postsynaptic cells Cadherin bridges the synapase from both sides We know that there is active signalling involving these bridges
These also keeps the nano-columns in place, such the the receptors and transmitters are kept just in the right places for effective signallingWhen an astrocyte surrounds a synapsis, which has metabotropic neurotransmitter receptors, which can release molecules, that can affect the post- and presynapse. The synapses form especially in the embryonic stage and the postal-natal period, but continue out entire lives.From the puberty we begins pruning the synapses Too much pruning might be a mechanism behind schitzophenia

item.title: Synaptic Plasticity
item.description:
Synaptic plasticity is an extremely central part of information processing and learningThe synaptic strength is defined as the possibility for changing the firering of the action potentials of the postsynaptic strength For excitatory synapsis is it the size of the EPSP For inhibitory synapsis is it the size of the IPSP The synapsis is stimulated very frequently - sometimes 100s of times a second This can change the strength of the synapsis - decreasing it step by step Facilitation: the stregth is increased by repetitive stimuli Depression: the strength is decreased by repetitive stimuli A synapsis can either have fascilitation and depression or both Post-tetanic potentiation - The increase of synaptic strength after a break in firering A synapse can have facilitation, depression or both Synaptic depression The depression is a physical property as a result of the readily releasable pool (RRP) decreasing in size, as the vesicle release is faster than the priming of vesicles in the presynaptic terminalSynaptic facilitation The facilitation might be a result of the residual in the presynaptic terminal, that is the left-over . This will stimulate the priming of vesicles, meaning, that the RRP will increase in size as more action potentials occur.
Sensory neuron: P fires multiple times after engaging in contact with something

item.title: Cell Membrane Structure
item.description:
Tags: #Proteins #Chemistry #CellBiology The membrane or lipid bilayer is one of the most important structures of the cells. Only 50 nm thick, it is about 1/10000 the thickness of paper. It is of course the outer border of the cell, known as the plasma membrane, but it is also used as an internal membrane in a wide range of organels including: Mitochondria (Both outer and inner membrane) Nucleus (Double membrane?) Peroxisomes Lysosomes Endosomes All kinds of transport vesicles Endoplasmatic reticulum Golgi apparatus When we talk about a membrane - this includes both the lipid bilayer, and the membrane proteins The common factor of all molecules in the membrane is that they are amphipathic meaning that they have both hydrophobic and hydrophillip parts.The main constituents is of course the membrane lipids. These can be further subdivided into three classesPhospholipids is the basic structure, making up for most of the membrane molecules in numbers (not weight). These consists of a hydrophilic head, which include a phosphate, linked to two hydrophobic lipid tails, formed from fatty acids. Commonly one tail is saturated (meaning no double bonds - hydrogen saturation), while the other is unsaturated (at least one double bond). The amount of saturation among the phospholipids affects the fluidity of the membrane - More saturated tails - less fluid. The double tail allows the phospholipids to combine into the sheets of the lipid bilayer, whereas single tail lipids (detergents) instead form spheres called micelles Sterols (usually cholesterol) consists of a hydrophilic head (hydroxyl group), a rigid planar hydrophobic steroid and a hydrophobic tail (hydrocarbon). The sterols decreases the fluidity of the membrane Glycolipids is similar to phospholipids, but instead of a phosphate based hydrophilic head, they have carbohydrates - often oligosaccharides and monosaccharides. These sugar structures can be composed in a wide range, and they thus play a role in identifying cells.
Proteins make up for about 50% of the weight of the membrane, although the ratio is about 50 lipids to 1 protein. They are responsible for most of the membrane functions. Transporters move specific molecules in and/or out of the compartment. This is often done inversely the the electrochemical gradient of the molecules, and thus they often require energy (ATP, coupled transport, etc.) - E.g. -pump Channels creates most of the permeability of the membrane, allowing the influx and efflux of specific molecules - E.g. the leak channels and the voltage-gated channels Anchors are proteins that binds to macromolecules on the inside, outside or both. - E.g. the integrins, which link intracellular actin filaments to extracellular matrix proteins Receptors that detects chemical signals, and relays them to the cells interior - E.g. growth factor (PDGF) receptor Enzymes, that catalyzes reactions on the membrane - E.g. adenylyl cyclase which catalyzes cyclic AMP in response to an extracellular signal (Sort of a receptor i guess) The membrane proteins can be subdivided into integral membrane proteins, which is an actual part of the membrane, and peripheral membrane proteins, which is attached to other membrane proteins, and thus can be more easily added or removed.
The integral membrane proteins can be transmembrane if they penetrate both monolayers of the lipid bilayer (Single-pass, double-pass, etc.), monolayer-assiciated if they are only present in one monolayer (either side), and lipid linked, if they are merely covalently linked to one or more membrane lipid.Because of the hydrophilic backbone of the proteins, they have to form specific conformations, that shields the backbone by hydrophobic side chains towards to lipid tails Single -helices with hydrophobic side chains can penetrate the bilaier Multiple -helices can form a pore by multiple amphipathic -helices forming a ring, with hydrophilic sides pointing inwards (towards the channel) and hydrophobic sides pointing outwards (towards the lipid bilayer)
A barrel can be formed of a sheet folded into a cylinder, with one side being hydrophilic and one side being hydrophobic The lipid bilayer of the membrane is kept together not by bindings, but by hydrophobic forces. Since both the intracellular and extracellular environments are aqueous, the hydrophobic tails of the membrane lipids is being pushed together, to minimize the thermodynamical energy cost of the cage-like structures formed by the water around the hydrophobic molecules. Because of the double tails, the lipids cant easily form small spheres, such as micelles, and instead form sheets of two layers - two hydrophilic sides, with a hydrophobic center. This large sheets then form compartments, to "shield" the hydrophobic sides:
The membrane is incredibly flexible as it can change shape, grow, and move without breaking. This is a result of the fluidity of the membrane. As the membrane lipids as not bound together, they are free to move in the two dimensional plane, that is the membrane - lipids and membrane proteins are know to move around - lateral diffusion, and rotate along the axis ortogonal to the membrane. They don't flip-flop across the bilayer spontainously (Once a month per lipid on average)
The fluidity is important for a number of reasons Fast diffusion of membrane proteins, which is import in protein interaction, and for the spread of proteins from the sites of insertion to the whole cell. Its an important part of membrane fusion The fluidity of the membrane is determined mainly by two factors: The length and saturation of the lipid tail Saturated tails allows the lipids to pack together tightly, increasing the resistance of movement in the membrane Plant fats are usually unsaturated and oils are therefore liquid, while animals fats and butter are more saturated and thus "solid". This is used in bacteria and yeast cells, which modulates saturation dependent on the temperature to keep a constant fluidity of the membrane The inclusion of sterols (in animals the is almost always cholesterol) The planar parts of the sterols fits the spaces left by the kinks of unsaturated tails, and thus decreases the flexibility (and permeability) The lipid bilayer is not symmetrical in composition. This is evident both for membrane lipids and membrane proteins. Most noticable is the glycolipids which is almost exclusively present in the extracellular space (lumen when inside the cell).
The same side of the membrane always points towards the cytosol. This means, that the extracellular side points inwards in the lumen when part of the ER and golgi apparatus, and is inwards when part of transport vesicles.
The membrane in animals is often reinforced by an interior cell cortex of protein filaments, which is attached to the membrane by the transmembrane proteins (anchors). An example is the cortex of the red blood cells, which gives them their concave shape.
Sometimes we want to keep some proteins in specific regions of the cell - for example the transports proteins responsible for the uptake of nutrients in the epithelial cells of the gut. That is we want to restrict the diffusion of the membrane proteins. This can be done in multiples ways A tight junction can act is a diffusion barrier, that stops proteins from moving past Extracellular matrix and cell cortex, can anchor the proteins in place Similarly proteins on a neighbour cell can keep each other in place
Just as the glycolipids, many of the transmembrane proteins have chains of sugars attached. Glycoproteins have oligosaccharides, while proteoglycans have long polysaccharide chains. Togther with the glycolipids these form the glycocalyx or carbohydrate layer. This sugar coating serves multiple purposes It protects the membrane against mechanical damage The sugars attracts water, which results in a slimy surface that decreases friction between cells - e.g. white blood cells, that needs to squeeze through small openings. They create a finger print of the cell type which can be recognized by other transmembrane proteins known as lectins The phospholipids are synthesizes by enzymes on the surface of the endoplasmatic reticulum. These membrane lipids are added to the cytosolic side of the ER bilayer. Since they don't flip-flop spontaneously, the movement to the other bilayer is catalyzed by scramblase - a type of transporter protein. Thus the phospholipids are evenly distributed among the layers. From here it is compartmentalized and distributed among other organelles - especially the golgi aparatus In the golgi membrane the asymmetry of the membrane is formed Another transporter protein called flippase flips specific phospholipids from the extracellular side, to the cytosol side More on the compartmentalization later!

item.description:
Tags: #CellBiology #Physiology
The plasma membrane controls all transport into and out of the cell, almost exclusively through simple diffusion, with the help of transmembrane proteins or through vesicles fusion (see Compartments and Protein Distribution).
Given the second law of thermodynamics, the molecules wants to spontaneously spread out as much as possible to decrease the order of the system. When looking at at divided system they wants to balance the concentrations meaning that the molecules moves towards the lowest concentration creating the concentration gradient. When combined with the electrical properties of charged particles, this creates the electrochemical gradient. The permeability of a membran without membrane proteins is what gives rise to simple diffusion. This is when molecules moves through the lipid bilayer directly. The rates of this happening is dependent on the size and polarity of the molecules. Small non-polar molecules dissolves readily in the lipid bilayer, and thus diffuse easily across the membrane - This include (32 Dalton), (44 Dalton) and Steroid hormones Small uncharged molecules does not dissolve in the lipid, but can sometimes diffuse across the bilayer - This includes (18 Dalton) and ethanol (46 Dalton) Larger uncharged molecules almost never diffuse across the membrane - This includes glucose (180 Daltons), amino acids and nucleosides For charged molecules, practically no diffusion takes place - The membrane is times more permeable to water than small ions ( and )
The proteins used for transporting molecules across the lipid bilayer can be divided into two groups:
Channels creates most of the permeability of the membrane, allowing the influx and efflux of specific molecules. This is the simplest mechanism of movement, as it is simply to create a hydrophilic "hole" in the hydrophobic wall that is the lipid bilayer.All channels mediate passive transport - the molecules follow their electrochemical gradient whether this is in or out of the membrane.Some of the simplest channels is the aquaporins, the makes the membrane permanently much more permeable to water.
These aquaporins are also responsible for the osmosis of the cell. The net flux of water is from the area of lowest concentration of solutes to the highest. If the inside concentration - or osmolarity, exceeds the extracellular solution, it creates an influx of water molecules, which means that the intracellular pressure increases. To combat this, and reach osmotic equilibrium, ion pumps, such as the -ATPase, removes solutes from the cell.Gated Channels Som channels have multiple conformations which involves a gate, and can thus be open or closed by specific triggers. These gates are often specified by two things The specification of the molecules that can pass the gate. This varies from a single type of ion, to large gates that allow everything up to macro molecules to pass (Such as the toxin aerolysin). In human cells, and especially neurons, ion channels are most common. The trigger necessary for changing the conformation and opening/closing the gate.
Mechanically-gated channels respons to mechanical forces such as extracellular objets or auditory waves Ligand-gated channels can respond to either extracellular or intracellular molecules (ligands)
Voltage-gated channels are present in all cells but especially in the neurons of the nervous system pH-gated channels Phosphorylation-gated channels

See Action Potential (NeuroFys) and Membrane Potential (NeuroFys) for more details on voltage gated channels.Transporters move specific molecules in/out of the compartment. A tranporter is differentiable from the channels by the property of changing shape in order to transport molecules.
Most transporters are passive transporters, meaning that they move molecules along their electrochemical gradient. An example of theis is the glucose transporter which by randomly changing between 12 conformations binds and releases glucose, such that on average it moves towards its concentration gradient (glucose doesn't have an electrical gradient).
The advantage of passive transporters over channels, is the specificity necessary for larger molecules - for example the glucose transporter can only tranpose the specific isomer L-Glucose and not D-Glucose. The disadvantage is of course the speed of the proces. Some ion channels allow milions of ions to pass each second, which is 1000 times faster, than the fastes known transporter.Transporters can also move molecules against their electrochemical, in which case they require energy (ATP, coupled transport, etc.) - E.g. -pumpThis is done using ATP-driven pumps and Gradient-driven pumps (coupled transporters) and Light-driven pumpsLight-driven pumps Uses the electromagnetic energy of the photon to transport out of the cell (only in microorganism)ATP-driven pumps Multiple ATP-driven pumps is present in the cell, but by far the most abundant is the -ATPase. Other pumps include The pump, that transports out of the cell The pump the creates the acidic environment of the lysozymes. In plants, bacteria and funghi a different type pump Sodium-Potassium Pump or -ATPasen creates the and gradients It uses of the ATP in an average animal cell When 3 sodium binds to the protein, it changes the conformation given the electrical charge This hydrolyzes the ATP, adding a phosphate with a high-energy linkage This creates conformational change, that allows the sodium to be released and 2 potassium to bind The protein is then dephosphorilized and returns to the original conformation, releasing the phosphate
Gradient-driven pumps Coupled transporters moves molecules (not just ions) against their gradients via the coupled molecules being moved towards their gradient
This is used for Capture of nutrients Release of metabolites Recapture of neurotransmitters The co-transport can be a symporter if the molecules moves in the same direction An example is the -coupled serotonin transporter, which drives the recapture of serotonin by a simultaneous intake of . item.title: Peripheral Nervous System (PNS)
item.description:
Tags: #Neuroanatomy #Neuroscience No synapses in the ganglion of the sensory PNS!Parts of the ANS is actually in the CNS, that is the preganglionic neurons.Mainly controls the viscera (Internal organs)Autonomic ganglia are clusters of nerve cell bodies located outside the central nervous system (CNS) that play a crucial role in the autonomic nervous system (ANS). These ganglia serve as relay stations where preganglionic neurons (part of CNS), originating from the CNS, synapse with postganglionic neurons that innervate target organs such as the heart, smooth muscles, and glands. There are two main types of autonomic ganglia: sympathetic ganglia, which are typically located near the spinal cord and are involved in the "fight or flight" response, and parasympathetic ganglia, which are usually found closer to or within the target organs and mediate the "rest and digest" functions. By integrating and modulating neural signals, autonomic ganglia ensure the appropriate regulation of involuntary physiological processes, maintaining homeostasis and enabling the body to respond effectively to internal and external changes.
The sympathetic nervous system (SNS) is the part of the body’s automatic control system that kicks into gear during stressful or exciting situations, often referred to as the "fight or flight" response. When activated, it prepares the body to face challenges by increasing energy and alertness. This system uses chemical messengers called neurotransmitters to communicate: preganglionic neurons release acetylcholine, which signals postganglionic neurons, and these neurons then release norepinephrine (Noradrenaline) to influence target organs like the heart, lungs, and blood vessels. As a result, the SNS triggers effects like a faster heartbeat, widened airways, and heightened focus, helping you react quickly to danger or pressure. By managing these rapid changes, the SNS ensures the body can handle stress and maintain balance in demanding situations.The parasympathetic nervous system (PSNS) is the calming counterpart to the sympathetic nervous system, often referred to as the "rest and digest" system. It works to conserve energy and promote relaxation, helping the body recover and maintain balance after stress or activity. The PNS uses neurotransmitters to communicate: preganglionic neurons release acetylcholine, which signals postganglionic neurons, and these neurons also release acetylcholine to influence target organs like the heart, digestive system, and salivary glands. This activation slows the heart rate, stimulates digestion, and encourages processes like nutrient absorption and waste elimination. By fostering a state of calm and restoration, the PNS ensures the body can recharge and function efficiently during periods of rest and recovery.
The Enteric Nervous System is a local network of sensory and motor neurons that regulates the functioning of the gut, under the control of the CNS. Because it regulates digestive activities of the gut, the enteric nervous system plays a key role in maintaining fluid and nutrient balances in the body.

The Central nervous is the part of the nervous system inside the spine and the cranium. It has a narrow fluid filled channel called the canalis central, which is surrounded by first grey matter and then white matter. Its surrounded by three meningial membranes called dura mater, pia mater, and arachnoidea mater. From medulla spinalis 31 pair of spinal nerves protrude.
The encephalon has three divisions - cerebellum, the brain stem or truncus encephalicus, and the fore brain or proencephalon. The brainstem consists of three parts:

item.title: Protein General Function and Enzymes
item.description:
Tags: #Proteins #Enzymes All proteins stick or bind to other molecules in a specific manner. This substance, whether it is an ion, an organic molecule or a macro molecules, is called a ligand. The high specificity of the binding of proteins is a result of the large set of non-covalent interactions between the ligand ond the protein, making it a relation between hand and glove. The region of the protein binding to the ligand is called the binding site formed by a physical cavity (or other shape) of the protein, and the arrangement of side chains in this area. These side chains often comes from amino acids far apart in the sequence, but close in proximity. Proteins often have multiple binding sites, some of which have external functionality, and some of which acts upon the protein it self (such as inhibition).The proteins have a variety of functions: Static, such as actin, which binds to other actin molecules to form filament. Movement for motor proteins such as kinesin, which binds to microtubulis Antibodies which binds to specific antigens, and signals specific protetion cells such as phagocytic cells (and many other functions) Enzymes catalyzes chemical reactions by binding to substrates (and products) Hella lot more functions An important class of proteins that catalyzes almost all chemical reactions in the cell, while retaining it's own structure. In general enzymes bind to one or more substrate, creates favorable conditions for a reaction that transform substrate to product which is then released from the enzyme.
Enzymes cannot make energetically unfavorable reactions happen, unless this is part of a coupled or sequential reaction, with a sum total negative . They can however catalyze energetically favorable reactions, that have a very high activation energy, meaning that they practically never happen freely in the cytosol. They do this by lowering the activation energy of the reaction, by hosting to right conditions in a variety of ways, and thus speeding up the reaction, often by a factor of one million or more.
The activation energy is lowered, by the binding site being a comfortable fit for the substrate to enter the transition state, in which the reaction can spontaneously happen. This is by the many non-covalent forces, that strains the bound substrate molecule, changes the partial electron distribution and molecule orientation.
Enzymes can catalyze reactions that bind multiple molecules, split single molecules or alter molecular structure. At low concentration of substrate, this is the governing factor, and as the concentration increases, the speed will converge towards , which is the maximum speed of the given concentration of enzymes. As it converges, it is difficult to determine the concentration of substrate at we describe the concentration at the speed called the Michealis constant - . A large indicates weak binding, while a small indicates strong binding. The speed can be described at a function of substrate concentration for a given enzyme concentration:
Some protein functions are a result a small non-protein molecules bound to the proteins. This could be retinal, that makes rhodopsin photoreceptive, and the iron containing heme of hemoglobin, that binds oxygen. In enzymes these non-protein molecules are often called coenzymes.

item.title: Protein Regulation and Dynamics
item.description:
Tags: #Proteins #Enzymes Most proteins and enzymes do not work continuously at full speed, but are regulated in a coordinated fashion. This regulation occurs at many levels: Gene expression control - regulates amount of protein produced Degredation of protein regulation Confinement of specific proteins to specific cellular compartments Rapid adjustment of the protein activity it self Enzymes usually have regulatory sites to which another molecules than the substrate binds, altering the rate at which the enzyme converts its substrate the product. There is often connections between substrates and regulatory molecules in a specific pathway, such as feedback inhibition, where the final product of a pathway doubles as an inhibitor of a previous enzyme, meaning that an abundance of final product slows the production of precursor substrate. Often times this is a network of multiple splitting pathways, with inhibitory products as illustrated:
Feedback inhibition is a form of negative regulation, but enzymes also has the property of binding to molecules, that speeds up the catalysis - positive regulation.Regulation of enzymes is called allostery - named after the greek for "other change". Many enzymes have at least two sites of binding, the active site and the regulatory site. When ligand binds to a regulatory site it goes trough a conformational change which slightly changes the structure. This can make the active site of the protein more or less accommodating of the substrate. Proteins with the ability to adopt two or more slightly different conformations, which regulates activity are called allosteric. This is not only enzymes, but many other proteins as well. Without the regulatory ligand, the protein will spontaneously interconvert between the two conformations (not necessarily 50/50), but with the regulatory ligand present, the enzyme will prefer the conformation, that fits it best, deeming the regulated conformation overwhelmingly abundant.
Another method of regulation involves binding a phosphate group to a side chain of the protein. The double negative charge of the phosphate can cause conformational change. This structural shift can affect the ability to bind ligands elsewhere. This use of reversible protein phosphorylation is abundant - about of the 10.000 proteins in the cell are phosphorylated at any one time. This system is connected to the states of the cell, for example controlling the division cycle.It involves an enzyme-catalyzed transfer of the terminal phosphate group of to the hydroxyl group of the following aminos:
The reaction is catalyzed by protein kinase. The reverse reaction called dephosphorylation is catalyzed by protein phosphatase. The phosphorylation can both inhibit or stimulate protein activity, depending on the protein. Hundreds of different protein kinases are responible for phosphorylating different proteins or sets of proteins, while a smaller set of protein phosphatase are responsible for the reverse reaction. Thus the phosphorylation is dependent on the activity of these proteins, which themselves are regulated in ways.For many enzymes, this phosphorylation and dephosphorylation happens in a swift cycle, which, even though it takes energy in the form of , allows rapid regulation. Many temporary protein alterations with covalent bindings are utilized in the cell. More than 100 of these modifications takes place in the cell by enzyme catalysis, some of the important are: Phosphorylation can also create docking sites for binding both other proteins, promoting complexes. Many proteins are modified by the addition of acetyl to lysine side chains, including histones. The addition of palmitate fatty acid to a cysteine side chain drives protein to associate with cell membranes. Attachment of ubiquitin (76-amino acid polypeptide) targets a protein for degradation. Many proteins have many sites of covalent modifications, for example the protein p53, which plays a role in responding to DNA damage, has 20 sites of modification - allowing an enormous variety of combinations, which gives great flexibility for the behavior of the protein. Covalent modifications allows the cell to make optimal use of proteins, and respond rapidly to changes in the environment. Instead of enzymatically transfered ATP, these proteins transfer phosphate as part of guinine nucleotide (Guanosine triphosphate), which is bound to the protein in its active conformation, hydrolyses a phosphate to switch to inactive, and then dissociates the GDP in a cycle.
These GDP-binding proteins act as molecular switches, which activates in response to cell signals, and then binds to other proteins to regulate their activity.A group of proteins utilize their range of conformations to drive movement. This is responsible for, among other things: Muscle contractions Moving organelles such as chromosomes during mitosis Moving macromolecules among cytoskeletal tracks The series of conformation these proteins undergo, must bo directional, as non regulated random conformational shift would result in average standstill. This is done using ATP-hydrolysis to make some steps irreversible, as the energy for the reverse conformational change is too large to happen spontaneously. The result being random conformational shifts and thereby movement on a small scale, but irreversible steps making the long-term process directional.
Many tasks in the cell is catalyzed by a highly coordinated, linked set og many proteins called a protein machine. For most of these machines, the hydrolysis of nucleoside triphosphates (ATP and GTP) drives an ordered series of conformational changes in some of the individual protein subunits, enabling an ensemble of coordinated movement - for example: Synthesis of proteins in ribosomes Replication and reperation of DNA These protein machines aren't rapidly produces spontaneously. Instead special scaffold proteins are used to catalyze this proces by binding to the proteins needed with its structure domains, while the unstructured regions are flexible, so that they collide in ways that result in the resulting protein complexes. This allows the cell to deploy scaffold proteins in the specific regions at the right time, and thus controll the production of protein machines. Some other scaffolds are not proteins but RNA scaffolds. Aggregates of proteins, RNAs and protein machinces, can become huge, creating distinct biochemical compartments in the cell without any membranes. This occurs when the macromolecule-macromolecule interaction becomes strong enough, and a phase seperation occurs. This produces enclosed regions with a special biochemical environment. The largest of these is the nucleolus, which is the "ribosome factory" where ribosomal RNAs are transcribed and ribosomal subunits are formed. Some intrecellular condensates are based on amyloid structures, reversible assemblies of sheets, that coems together to produce a hydrogel that pulls other molecules into the condensate.

item.title: Protein Structures and Shapes
item.description:
Tags: #Proteins #ChemistryBy far the most prevalent molecules in the cell in terms of dry mass providing shape and structure to the cell, intracellular chemical reactions as enzymes, transporters and channels through the membranes, signalling inter- and intracellular, and a vast list of machinery parts with various functions. One classification of proteins: Enzymes catalyze covalent bond breakage or formation Structural Proteins provides mechanical support - E.g. Collagen Transport Proteins carry small molecules - E.g. Hemoglobin Motor Proteins generates movement - E.g. Myosin Storage Proteins store amino acids or ions - E.g. Casein in milk Signal Proteins carry extracellular signals - E.g. Insulin Receptor Proteins detects signals and transmits them - E.g. Acetylcholin receptor and Rhodopsin (Light sensitive) Transcription Regulators binds to DNA to switch genes on and off Special-Purpose Proteins - E.g. Flourescent protein Amino acids are molecules recognized by the tertiary carbon with an amino group (), a carboxyl group (), a hydrogen and a side chain. Many amino acids exist, but only 20 are a part of the proteins in humans.
The amino terminus are called the N-terminus, and are drawn to the left, while the carboxyl terminus or C-terminus are drawn to the right. The side chain have a variety of functions, some being hydrophobic, some having electrical charge, and some able to form special covalent bonds with other side chains.The ionization of the amino group and carboxyl group is dependent on the pH of the environment (cytosol):
All 20 common amino acids are show in the following table:
The amino acids form peptide bonds between the amino group and the carboxyl group through a condensation reaction. The organization of amino acids in the sequences of the polypeptide chains is called the primary structure of the proteins, with an N-terminus and a C-terminus. The peptide bonds are rotation-locked, meaning that it can be a cis bond or a trans bond. Because of the steric clashes (too small van der waal radius) of the side groups of the amino acids, the trans peptide bonds are much more common. Insert figure The bonds between the -carbon and the amino group and carboxyl group respectively are free to rotate, though some combinations of rotations are energetically favorable. The angle of rotation of the amino group is called (Phi) and the angle of rotation of the carboxyl group is called (Psi).
The favorable combinations are found experimentally and shown in this Ramachandram plot:
This ramachandram plot is general, but there also exists independent plots for each amino acidGiven the flexibility of the rotation of the bonds, the peptide chains can fold in an enormous number of ways. The shape is constrained by a number of non-covalent bonds. The secondary structure, is a description of the regularly repeating structure in the peptide chain. Such include -helices, -pleated sheets, -turns, and -turns.The helix is common because it's formed by the peptide backbone and not the side chains. It exists in two mirror forms - the abundant right-handed -helix (show in figure below) and the rare left-handed -helix. The helix is formed by hydrogen bonds between every fourth amino acid, formed between the N-H of the amino group and the O=C of the carboxyl group (ketone in the chain). This pattern forms a full turn every 3.6 amino acid with a distance of 0.54 nm (Or 5.4 Å).
-helices are abundant in membrane proteines, as the polar peptide backbone can be shielded by hydrophobic side chains protruding on the outside of the helix.Two (or three) -helices can form together to a coiled-coil structure, when they have hydrophobic side chains on one side of the helix, which can be faced inwards in against hydrophobic side of the other helix (helices) and twist around each other minimizing cytosol contact. These are present in -keratin (hair, skin) and myosin (muscles), and they give wool fibers their extraordinary property of regaining their structure after stretching.Just as the -helix, the formation of -sheets only rely on the peptide backbone and not the side chains. The backbone in each strand is roughly planar, with side chains protruding to alternating sides of the plane. Each -sheet consists of multiple parallel and antiparallel strands, keeping each other in place with hydrogen bonding: The antiparallel strands connect directly across - as the strands run in opposite directions, the amino acids are flipped, and the N-H and C=O can form hydrogen bonds to the opposite amino acid The parallel strands cant form direct bonds as the strands run in the same direction, so the N-H forms hydrogen bond the the C=O in an amino acid adjacent to the left, while the C=O forms bond to an amino acid on the right.
The sheets can come together purely parallel, purely antiparallel or a mix. The distance between aminos in the -strands is 0.34 nm (in contrast to 0.15 nm in the -helix). The shape of the -sheet can be planar, but often it is somewhat twisted:
It is a structural important element of many proteins - it gives silk fibers the tensile strength (resistance to pull) and form the basis of amyloid structures. Turns are not regularly repeating structures, but are analyzed on the secondary structure level. The reverse turn (-turn or hairpin turn) is a structure with a hydrogen bond between the backbone of two amino acids spaced three paces apart, and outwards protruding side chains.
The -loop is defined as a larger structure, with more aminos in between the loop neck. Loops are mostly present on the surface of proteins.Though all amino acids partake in these substructure, there is a difference in frequency, which can help predict shape:
The final shape called the conformation is determined energetically, by the shape that minimizes its free energy (G). Thus the folding process releases heat and decreases entropy. A number of bonds plays a part in determining the conformation of the chains: Hydrogen bonds between polar side chains or the amino and carboxyl groups Electrostatic attractions between electrically charged side chains or partially charged polar groups Van der waals attraction - both pushing and pulling Hydrophobic forces - non-polar side chains being forced together to the inside in aqueous environments As a general rule of thumb - non polar side chains points inwards, whereas polar side chains point outwards, unless hydrogen bonded to other side chains or the peptide backbone.
However, some proteins reside in hydrophobic environments such as membranes, and form structures with a hydrophobic shell and polar internal structures, such as this membrane channel, porin:
Some polypeptide chains fold into two or more compact regions that may be connected by a flexible segment of polypeptide chain. These compact units, called domains, range in size from about 30 to 400 amino acid residues. Larger proteins contain more than one polypeptide chain. In these proteins each polypeptide chain called a subunit is connected at certain binding sites by non-covalent bonding. These larger structures can consist of similar repeating subunits. A dimer is the simplest case with two identical chains in a symmetrical complex, such as the CAP protein. If the subunits have two complementary binding sites, manu subunits can form helices or rings, depending on the angles.
An abundant example of this is Actin which forms helix structures, and forms a major filament system in the cytoskeleton. Other large structures that form are tubes such as microtubules and spherical shells such as virus vectors. The proteins forming individual units are called globular proteins, but the ones forming long repeating structure are called fibrous proteins. These sort of fibrous filaments also play a role in forming the extracellular matrix, especially collagen molecules.These larger structure often include other molecules than poplypetide chains such as RNA, DNA and non-organic molecules such as the heme in hemoglobin.The sequence of amino acids solely determines the final conformation, and proteins that has been denatured by urea (disrupting non-covalent bonds) and -mercaptoethanol (reduces disulfide bonds) for example will often recover it conformation after the urea is removed (renaturation).Protein folding is generally catalyzed by chaperone proteins, which speeds up the proces of finding the energetically favorable pathway. Some of these binds to the partially folded structures, while others completely encase the polypeptide chains.Covalent disulfide bonds between the side chains of cysteine (and other less common covalent bonds). These bonds does not dictate conformation, but keeps it stable.
Sometimes proteins fold incorrectly, putting them out of function. However, sometimes thay form amyloid structure that can damage cells and tissues. These contribute to neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer's and Huntington's disease. Another dangerous misfolding are proteins called prions. These are self-replicating in the sense that they convert the correctly folded versions to its own misfolded version (zombie-proteins) which then aggregates. This include scrapie in sheep, bovine spongiform encephalopahty (mad cows disease) in cattle and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in humans. In contrast to amyloid structure diseases, prions are infectious.

#Neuroscience #Chemistry #TransmittersPsychopharmacology is the neuropsychological effects of medication on behavior and the function of the central nervous system.
In the field of cognitive neuroscience, Cognitive Psychopharmacology can improve our understanding of normal behavior, and the connections between neuroanatomy and neurochemistry. In Animal models we use lesion studies, as often as possible with reversible, functional lesions by blocking single neurotransmitter systems or by doing up- or down regulation of transmissions. There exists a large variety of neurotransmitters (more than 60), so in order to have a clear understanding of what kind of molecules we are categorizing as transmitters, there is a criterion list: The substance exists in presynaptic axon terminals. The presynaptic cell contains appropriate enzymes for synthesizing the substance. The substance is released in significant quantities when action potentials reachthe terminals of the presynaptic cell. Specific receptors that recognize the released substance exist on the postsynaptic membrane. Experimental application of the substance produces changes in postsynaptic cells. Blocking release of the substance prevents presynaptic activity from affecting the postsynaptic cell. #Neuroscience Learning objectives
Hormones are chemicals secreted by endocrine glands into the blood stream. These hormones travel through your blood to other cells and are taken up by receptor molecules in target cells.The discovery of hormones:
The endocrine system is one of the chemical communicative systems in the body
Hormones are produces in the endocrine glands
The blending of neural and endocrine functions in one cell
A Neuroedocrine cell, releasing hormones into the bloodstream as a reaction following an action potential - an example of the mix of endocrine and neural acticity Amine: 1-2 amino acids Peptides: Many amino acids Bind to specific recepters on the membrane, altering the cell function with non-genetic action Steroid: Able to permeate membranes, and thus acts on intracellular recepters - often entering the nucleus with the recepter stating a protein production with genomic action. Needs a cofactor

Both "releasing hormones" and "tropic hormones" are leased in the process of releasing actual hormones in the endocrine glands.
Hormone with the only purpose to control the release of another hormone.In the hypothalamus Releasing hormones CORTICOTROPIN-RELEASING HORMONE (CRH) THYROTROPIN-RELEASING HORMONE (TRH) GONADOTROPIN-RELEASING HORMONE (GnRH) GROWTH HORMONE-RELEASING HORMONE (GHRH) Inhibiting hormones when released from the hypothalamus SOMATOSTATIN (inhibits secretion of various hormones, e.g. GH, insulin, etc.) DOPAMINE (inhibits prolactine release) Feedback systems
In the posterior Piuitary Two main hormones Oxytocin - Related to reproductive behaviour, released when taking care of children, etc. ARGININE VASOPRESSIN (APV; vasopressin; antidiuretic hormone ADH) - Increases blood-pressure (Releases water into the blood stream) The tropic hormones are stores in the axon terminals of the hyopothalamic-hypiophyseal tract in the posterior lobe of the pituitary glands.
In the anterior Piuitary Tropic hormones (Targets the endocrine glands - they are a intermedium of sorts) FSH LH TSH ACTH Nontropic hormones (Targets are the actual tissue - they are the "final" hormone) Prolactin MSH A mix of both GH
For example the oxytocin and prolactin system when feeding a baby:
The "anti-stress" glands of the body - Fight or flight mechanism
The Medulla secretes the catecholamines (the fast response): Adrenaline Noradrenialine This has the effect to prepare the body for action, raising heart rate, raising respiration, slowing gut function, etc.The Cortex secretes adrenocorticois Glucocoticoids (e.g. cortisol) Mineralocorticoids (aldostreone) Sex steriods (adrostenedione - gives male and female apperence) Cortisol is quite important It helps maintaining glucose balance in interaction with insuline It boosts the immune system (Seen when you get sick after a period of stress - for example during exam days etc.)

EFFECT on HIPPOCAMPAL VOLUME: Reduction in size. EFFECT on COGNITION: Impairment in thinking and memory. Secondary, impairment of cognitive function, and depression

#Neuroscience #PhysiologyIons that are "dissolved" in the intra- and extracellular fluids: , , and Repulsive forces: Same charge (+ & +, - & -)Attractive force: Opposite charge (+ & -)Current (Ampere - mA): Number of charged particles that flow through a given surface per time unit Potential (Voltages - mV): Amount of work energy required to move a unit of charged particles (Difference in charge across membrane) Diffusion: The net movement of anything generally from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. (Diffusion is driven by a gradient in Gibbs free energy or chemical potential.) That is, they move down their concentration gradient A membrane stops/slows the diffusion, but some particles can still cross based on the permeability of the membrane - The cell wall in it self has some amount of permeability, although low, but the neuron have selective permeability and it comes from different types of gates in the cell membrane.The sodium-potassium pump constantly switches sodium for potassium across the membrane, which in collaboration with the open potassium gates, lowers the potential across the membrane, until an equilibrium is reached - called the resting membrane potential

The resting potential can at equilibrium be calculated with the goldmand equation to approximately -65 mV:
When depolarization happens across a certain threshold, voltage-gated channels opens which rapidly depolarizes and "overshoots" up to 45 mV, where the channels close again, and gated channelse open and repolarizes the cell (hyperpolarization, acutally as it becomes even more polarized, than the resting potential, hindering further action potentials).
The action potential has to be propagated along the axon (about 10 m/s):

This is done at different speeds related to factors, such as size but mostly myelination, as the action potential in this case doesn't propogate gradually allong the axon, but instead it jumps between the Nodes of Ranvier (about 150 m/s):
The size of current "injected" to the cell doesn't change the size of the action potentials, as they are of the all-or-nothing type. However This changes the frequency of fired action potentials:

The action potential ends in the axon terminals where it reached the SynapsesExcitatory Postsynaptic Potentials (EPSPs) and Inhibitory Postsynaptic Potentials (IPSPs) are transient changes in the membrane potential of a neuron that occur in response to neurotransmitter binding at the synapse. EPSPs are depolarizing events, typically caused by the opening of ligand-gated ion channels (e.g., AMPA receptors) that allow Na+ influx, bringing the membrane potential closer to the threshold for firing an action potential. In contrast, IPSPs are hyperpolarizing events, often resulting from the opening of Cl- or K+ channels (e.g., GABA receptors), which make the membrane potential more negative and reduce the likelihood of an action potential. The balance between EPSPs and IPSPs determines whether a neuron will fire, playing a critical role in neural communication and information processing.There are two ways for different EPSP and IPSP to add up, both spatially with multiple synapses and temporally with synapses firering multiple times at a high frequency:
The action potential threshold is reached as a result of multiple EPSP, however the signaling og EPSP and IPSP strength is also determined by the distance from axon-hillock where the actual action potential is fired down the axon.

Feedback/Feed-forward-loops in between neurons is the systematic constellation of neurons in things such as soma sensory stimuli an olfactory stimuli, which allows us to adjust the the sensation to only be active at the beginning and the end of the stimuli, and being able differ between closely linked smells.
Mirror neurons are a type of brain cell that fires both when an individual performs an action and when they observe the same action performed by another. Discovered in the early 1990s, these neurons are thought to play a crucial role in understanding others' actions, intentions, and emotions, contributing to empathy, learning, and social interactions. Their discovery has significantly influenced research in neuroscience, psychology, and even artificial intelligence. - Giacomo Rizzolatti, Leonardo Fogassi, and Vittorio Gallese
